Takeminakata was also held to be the mythical ancestor of certain families who once served at the shrine as priests, foremost among them being the [[Suwa clan]], the high priests of the Upper Shrine of Suwa who were also revered as [[Arahitogami|living]] [[Shintai|vessels]] of the god.

Whereas in the ''[[Kojiki]]'' (ca. 712 CE) and later derivative accounts, Takeminakata appears as one of the sons of the god [[Ōkuninushi]] who fled to {{ill|Lake Suwa|ar|بحيرة سوا|arz|بحيره سوا|ceb|Suwa Ko|de|Suwa-See|eo|Suŭa-Lago|es|Lago Suwa|et|Suwa järv|eu|Suwa aintzira|fa|دریاچه سووا|fr|Lac Suwa|id|Danau Suwa|ja|諏訪湖|ko|스와호|lt|Suva (ežeras)|mk|Сува by the warrior god [[Takemikazuchi]], other myths (mostly of medieval origin) instead offer alternative explanations regarding the god of Suwa Shrine's origins and identity, portraying him either as an interloper who conquered Suwa by defeating the local ''kami'' of the region, as a king from ==Name==
[[File:Suwa Hosshō Banner - 諏訪法性旗.png|thumb|right|135px|Reproduction of {{ill|Takeda Shingen|ar|تاكيدا شين-غن|az|Takeda Şingen|ban|Takeda Shingen|ca|Takeda Shingen|cs|Šingen Takeda|de|Takeda Shingen|eo|Takeda Shingen|es|Takeda Shingen|fa|تاکدا شینگن|fi|Takeda Shingen|fr|Takeda Shingen|hak|Takeda Shingen|he|טקדה שינגן|hu|Takeda Singen|id|Takeda Shingen|it|Takeda Shingen|ja|武田信玄|jv|Takeda Shingen|ko|다케다 신겐|nl|Takeda Shingen|no|Takeda Shingen|pl|Shingen Takeda|pt|Takeda Shingen|ru|Такэда Сингэн|sk|Šingen Takeda|sq|Takeda Shingen|sr|Такеда Шинген|sv|Takeda Shingen|th|ทาเกดะ ชิงเง็ง|tr|Takeda Shingen|uk|Такеда Шінґен|vi|Takeda Shingen|wuu|武田信玄|zh|武田信玄|zh_min_nan|Takeda Singen|zh_yue|武田信玄|zu|Takeda Shingen|qid=Q276404|lt=Takeda Shingen}}'s Suwa Hosshō banner (諏訪法性旗). The inscription reads: ''[[:wikt:南無#Japanese|Namu]] Suwa Nangū Hosshō Kamishimo'' (or ''Jōge'') ''Daimyōjin'' (南無諏方南宮法性上下大明神)]]
The god is named 'Takeminakata-no-Kami' ({{nihongo2|建御名方神}}) in both the ''[[Kojiki]]'' (ca. 712 CE) and the ''[[Kujiki|''Sendai Kuji Hongi'']]'' (ca. 807-936 CE).<ref name="Hongi2">{{cite web|title=先代舊事本紀卷第四|url=http://miko.org/~uraki/kuon/furu/text/sendaikuji/sendaikuji04.htm|website=私本 先代舊事本紀}}</ref><ref name="Hongi">''Sendai Kuji Hongi'', Book 4 (先代舊事本紀 巻第四), in {{cite book|editor=Keizai Zasshisha|title=Kokushi-taikei, vol. 7 (国史大系 第7巻)|date=1898|publisher=Keizai Zasshisha|pages=243–244|url=http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/991097/136}}</ref> Variants of the name found in the imperially commissioned [[Rikkokushi|national histories]] and other literary sources include the following:<ref>{{Cite web|title=南方刀美神社|url=http://21coe.kokugakuin.ac.jp/db/jinja/240101.html|access-date=2020-12-05|website=神道・神社史料集成 (Shinto Jinja Database)|publisher=Kokugakuin University}}</ref>

* Minakatatomi-no-Kami (南方刀美神)
* Minakatatomi-no-Mikoto-no-Kami (御名方富命神)
* Takeminakatatomi-no-Mikoto (健御名方富命 / 建御名方富命)
* Takeminakatatomi-no-Mikoto-no-Kami (建御名方富命神)

The etymology of the name '(Take)minakata(tomi)' is unclear. While most commentators seem to agree that ''take-'' (and probably ''-tomi'') are honorifics, they differ in how to interpret the other components of the name. Some of the proposed solutions are as follows.

*The {{ill|Edo period|ar|فترة إيدو|ast|Periodu Edo|az|Edo dövrü|bcl|Panahon nin Edo|be|Перыяд Эда|bg|Едо (период)|bn|এদো যুগ|bo|ཨེ་དོའི་དུས་སྐབས།|br|Marevezh Edo|ca|Període Edo|ckb|سەردەمی ئێدۆ|cs|Období Edo|cv|Эдо тапхăрĕ|da|Edo-perioden|de|Edo-Zeit|el|Περίοδος Έντο|eo|Epoko de Edo|es|Período Edo|et|Edo ajastu|eu|Edo aroa|fa|دوره ادو|fi|Edo-kausi|fr|Époque d'Edo|gl|Período Edo|he|תקופת אדו|hi|एदो अवधी|hr|Edo (razdoblje)|hu|Edo-kor|id|Zaman Edo|is|Jedótímabilið|it|Periodo Edo|ja|江戸時代|jv|Jaman Édo|ko|에도 시대|lt|Edo laikotarpis|lv|Edo periods|mk|Едо (период)|mn|Эдогийн эрин|ms|Zaman Edo|new|इदो काल|nl|Edoperiode|nn|Edotida|oc|Periòde Edo|pl|Edo (okres)|pt|Período Edo|ro|Perioada Edo|ru|Период Эдо|simple|Edo period|sk|Obdobie Edo|sl|Obdobje Edo|sq|Periudha Edo|sr|Едо период|su|Période Edo|sv|Edoperioden|th|ยุคเอโดะ|tl|Panahong Edo|tok|tenpo pi kulupu lawa Eto|tr|Edo Dönemi|uk|Період Едо|ur|ایڈو دور|uz|Edo davri|vi|Thời kỳ Edo|war|Panahon Edo|wuu|江戶時代|zh|江户时代|zh_min_nan|Edo sî-tāi|zh_yue|江戶時代|qid=Q184963|lt=Edo period}} ''{{ill|Kokugaku|ar|كوكوجاكو|ast|Kokugaku|bg|Кокугаку|ca|Kokugaku|de|Kokugaku|es|Kokugaku|fa|کوکوگاکو|fi|Kokugaku|fr|Kokugaku|gl|Kokugaku|hu|Kokugaku|id|Kokugaku|it|Kokugaku|ja|国学|ko|국학 (일본사)|ms|Kokugaku|pt|Kokugaku|ru|Кокугаку|sah|Кокугаку|tr|Kokugaku|uk|Кокуґаку|zh|國學 (日本)|qid=Q855159|lt=Kokugaku}}'' scholar {{ill|Motoori Norinaga|ar|موتوري نوريناغا|bg|Мотоори Норинага|de|Motoori Norinaga|es|Motoori Norinaga|fa|موتوئوری نوریناگا|fi|Motoori Norinaga|fr|Motoori Norinaga|gl|Motoori Norinaga|hu|Motoori Norinaga|it|Motoori Norinaga|ja|本居宣長|ka|მოტოორი ნორინაგა|ko|모토오리 노리나가|lt|Norinaga Motoori|mt|Motoori Norinaga|pl|Norinaga Motoori|pt|Motoori Norinaga|ro|Motoori Norinaga|ru|Мотоори Норинага|simple|Motoori Norinaga|sl|Motoori Norinaga|th|โมโตริ โนรินางะ|tr|Motoori Norinaga|uk|Мотоорі Норінаґа|zh|本居宣長|qid=Q384647|lt=Motoori Norinaga}}<ref name="Norinaga2">Motoori, Norinaga (1937). [http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/1109355/81 古事記傳 (''Kojiki-den''), vol. 14] in Motoori Toyokai (ed.), ''Motoori Norinaga Zenshū'' (本居宣長全集), vol. 2. Tokyo: Yoshikawa Kōbunkan. p. 675. (Original work written 1764–1798)</ref> explained both ''take-'' (建) and ''mi-'' (御) as honorifics (称名 ''tatae-na''), with ''kata'' (方) as yet another ''tatae-na'' meaning "hard" or "firm" (堅). [[:en:Basil Chamberlain|Basil Chamberlain]] followed Motoori's lead and rendered the god's name as 'Brave-August-Name-Firm' in his translation of the ''Kojiki''.<ref name="Chamberlain">Chamberlain, Basil (trans.) (1882). [http://sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj039.htm Section XXXII.—Abdication of the Deity Master-of-the-Great-Land.] ''A translation of the "Ko-ji-ki" or Records of Ancient Matters.'' Yokohama: Lane, Crawford & Co.</ref>

Takeminatomi Shrine] (多祁御奈刀弥神社) stands.<ref>Ōta (1926). p. 8.</ref> [[:ja:大和岩雄|Ōwa Iwao]] (1990) suggests that the presence of [[Azumi people]] in both Awa and Shinano, as well as the possible connection between the Azumi and the Lower Shrine of Suwa, may explain the similarity between 'Takeminakata(tomi)' and 'Takeminatomi'.<ref>Ōwa (1990). pp. 214–216.</ref>
*''Minakata'' has also been linked to the [[Munakata Taisha|Munakata]] (宗像) of [[Kyushu]].<ref name="Yoshii">{{Citation|title = Takeminakata-no-Kami (建御名方神)|author=Yoshii, Iwao|encyclopedia = Encyclopedia Nipponica|year=1994 |volume=14|publisher=Shōgakukan|isbn=978-4-09-526114-0}}</ref> [[:ja:松岡静雄|Matsuoka Shizuo]] (1936) interpreted Minakatatomi as originally being a goddess – citing the fact that the deities of Munakata shrine were female – that was later conflated with the male god Takeminakata.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Matsuoka|first1=Shizuo|title=Minzokugaku yori mitaru Azuma-uta to Sakimori-uta (民族學より見たる東歌と防人歌)|date=1936|publisher=Ōokayama-shoten|pages=197–199|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QLb0QBVHZW8C}}</ref>
*Another explanation proposes ''minakata'' to mean "south(ern)" (南方).<ref>Miyaji (1931). p. 10.</ref> A variant of this hypothesis sees the name as hinting at a connection between the god and {{ill|Metalworking|af|Metaalbewerking|ar|صنع الأدوات المعدنية|ast|Metalistería|az|Metal emalı|be|Металаапрацоўка|bg|Металообработка|ca|Treball dels metalls|cs|Kovodělnictví|cy|Metelwaith|da|Metalarbejde|de|Metallverarbeitung|el|Μεταλλοτεχνία|eo|Metalfarado|es|Metalistería|eu|Metalgintza|fa|فلزکاری|fi|Metallintyöstö|he|עיבוד מתכת|hi|धातुकार्य|hr|Obrada metala|id|Pengerjaan logam|it|Lavorazione dei metalli|ja|金属加工|ko|금속가공|lv|Metālapstrāde|mk|Металообработка|nl|Metaalbewerking|pl|Obróbka metali|pt|Indústria metalmecânica|ru|Металлообработка|sh|Obrada metala|simple|Metalworking|sr|Obrada metala|sv|Metallbearbetning|te|లోహక్రియ|th|การแปรรูปโลหะ|tr|Metal işçiliği|uk|Металообробка|vi|Gia công cơ khí|zh|金屬加工|zh_min_nan|Kim-sio̍k ka-kang|zh_yue|金工|qid=Q953045|lt=Metalworking}}, in which the southern direction is important: [[:ja:真弓常忠|Mayumi Tsunetada]] (1981) for instance proposed that Takeminakata's name refers to the southern pillar of a ''takadono'' (a high-roofed house housing a ''{{ill|Tatara (furnace)|es|Tatara|fa|تاتارا (کوره)|fr|Tatara|it|Tatara|ja|たたら製鉄|ko|타타라|pl|Tatara|pt|Tatara (fornalha)|tt|Tatara|uk|Татара|vi|Tatara|zh|吹踏鞴|qid=Q3131218|lt=tatara}}'' furnace).<ref>{{Cite book|title = Nihon kodai saishi to tetsu (日本古代祭祀と鉄)|last1=Mayumi|first1=Tsunetada|publisher=Gakuseisha|page=110|year=1981}}</ref> Gustav Heldt's translation of the ''Kojiki'' (2014), where the name is translated as 'Brave Southward Smelter', follows this interpretation.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Heldt |first1=Gustav |title=The Kojiki: An Account of Ancient Matters |date=2014 |publisher=Columbia University Press |pages=46, 210 |isbn=9780231163880 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RAMZBQAAQBAJ}}</ref>
*Yet another theory interprets ''mi(na)-'' to mean "water" (水), pointing to the god being a [[:en:Water deity|Water deity]] perhaps associated with {{ill|Lake Suwa|ar|بحيرة سوا|arz|بحيره سوا|ceb|Suwa Ko|de|Suwa-See|eo|Suŭa-Lago|es|Lago Suwa|et|Suwa järv|eu|Suwa aintzira|fa|دریاچه سووا|fr|Lac Suwa|id|Danau Suwa|ja|諏訪湖|ko|스와호|lt|Suva (ežeras)|mk|Сува (езеро)|my|ဆုဝကန်|nn|Suwasjøen|pl|Suwa (jezioro)|ro|Lacul Suwa|ru|Сува (озеро)|sr|Језеро Сува|th|ทะเลสาบซูวะ|tr|Suwa Gölü|vi|Hồ Suwa|zh|諏訪湖|zh_yue|諏訪湖|qid=Q1206692|lt=Lake Suwa}}.<ref name="Yamaguchi">{{cite book|author=Yamaguchi, Yoshinori and Kōnoshi, Takamitsu (eds.)|title=Shinpen nihon koten bungaku zenshū, vol. 1. ''Zenkoku jinja saijin goshintokki'' (全国神社祭神御神徳記), quoted in Muraoka (1969). p. 14.</ref><ref name="Miyasaka31">Miyasaka, Mitsuaki (1987). "Kyodai naru kami no kuni. *An alternative explanation for the word ''-tomi'' (as well as the ''-tome'' in '[[Yasakatome]]', the name of this god's consort) is to link it with dialectal words for "snake" (''tomi'', ''tobe'', or ''tōbe''), thereby seeing the name as hinting to the god being a kind of {{ill|Snake worship|az|İlana sitayiş (totemizm)|bcl|Pagsamba sa halas|fa|مارپرستی|fi|Käärmeenpalvonta|fr|Culte du serpent|km|នាគខ្មែរ និង នាគសាសនា|ml|സർപ്പാരാധന|ru|Змеепоклонство|simple|Snake worship|sv|Ormkult|th|การบูชางู|vi|Tục thờ rắn|qid=Q3249489|lt=serpentine}} water deity (''[[mizuchi]]'').<ref>Tomiku, Takashi (1970). ''Himiko'' (卑弥呼). Gakuseisha. p. 48, cited in Kanai (1982). p. 6.</ref>

===''Suwa Daimyōjin''===
{{see also|Myōjin}}

During the medieval and early modern periods, the god enshrined in [[Suwa-taisha|Suwa Grand Shrine]] – specifically, in the Upper Shrine (''Kamisha'') located southeast of {{ill|Lake Suwa|ar|بحيرة سوا|arz|بحيره سوا|ceb|Suwa Ko|de|Suwa-See|eo|Suŭa-Lago|es|Lago Suwa|et|Suwa järv|eu|Suwa aintzira|fa|دریاچه سووا|fr|Lac Suwa|id|Danau Suwa|ja|諏訪湖|ko|스와호|lt|Suva (ežeras)|mk|Сува (езеро)|my|ဆုဝကန်|nn|Suwasjøen|pl|Suwa (jezioro)|ro|Lacul Suwa|ru|Сува (озеро)|sr|Језеро Сува|th|ทะเลสาบซูวะ|tr|Suwa Gölü|vi|Hồ Suwa|zh|諏訪湖|zh_yue|諏訪湖|qid=Q1206692|lt=Lake Suwa}} – was popularly known as ''Suwa Daimyōjin'' ({{nihongo2|諏訪大明神}} / 諏方大明神) or ''Suwa Myōjin'' ({{nihongo2|諏訪明神}}), a name also applied via {{ill|Metonymy|ar|كناية|az|Metonimiya|bcl|Metonimya|be|Метанімія|be_x_old|Мэтанімія|bg|Метонимия|bn|লক্ষণা (বাক্যালঙ্কার)|ca|Metonímia|cs|Metonymie|cy|Trawsenwad|da|Metonymi|de|Metonymie|el|Μετωνυμία|eo|Metonimio|es|Metonimia|et|Metonüümia|eu|Metonimia|fa|کنایه|fi|Metonymia|fr|Métonymie|gan|轉喻|gl|Metonimia|he|מטונימיה|hi|उपलक्षण|hr|Metonimija|ht|Metonimi|hu|Metonímia|ia|Metonymia|id|Metonimia|io|Metonimio|is|Nafnskipti|isv|Metonimija|it|Metonimia|ja|換喩|kaa|Metonimiya|kk|Метонимия|ko|환유|ky|Метонимия|la|Metonymia|lb|Metonymie|lt|Metonimija|lv|Metonīmija|mk|Метонимија|nl|Metonymie|nn|Metonym|no|Metonymi|oc|Metonimia|pa|ਮੈਟੋਨਮੀ|pl|Metonimia|pnb|کنایہ|pt|Metonímia|ro|Metonimie|ru|Метонимия|sah|Метонимия|scn|Mitunìmia|sd|ڪنايو|sh|Metonimija|simple|Metonymy|sk|Metonymia|sl|Metonimija|sq|Metonimia|sr|Метонимија|sv|Metonymi|ta|ஆகு பெயர்|th|นามนัย|tr|Mecâz-ı mürsel|tt|Метонимия|uk|Метонімія|ur|کنایات|uz|Metonimiya|vi|Hoán dụ|wa|Stindaedje do sinse|wuu|转喻|zh|轉喻|zh_yue|借代|qid=Q41966|lt=Metonymy}} to the shrine itself. The name '(Take)minakata(tomi)' was rarely used, if at all, during this period: indeed, medieval documents from Suwa Shrine simply refer to the god as ''sonshin'' / ''sonjin'' (尊神, "revered deity") or ''{{ill|Myōjin|fr|Myōjin|ja|明神|ko|묘진|zh|明神|qid=Q5369590|lt=Myōjin}}'' (明神, "bright deity" or "manifest deity").<ref>Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai, ed. (1995). p. 688.</ref> This however is hardly unusual, as before the early modern period use of titles such as ''myōjin'' or ''[[gongen]]'' for various gods and their shrines were so widespread that these deities were rarely referred to by their classical names.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Nakamura|first1=Issei|title=平安期における大明神号の成立とその意義 (The Formation and Significance of the Title Daimyoujin in the Heian Period)|journal=The Bukkyo University Graduate School Review. Compiled by the Graduate School of Literature.|date=2009-03-01|issue=37|page=74|url=http://archives.bukkyo-u.ac.jp/repository/baker/rid_DB003700003047}}</ref>

Other epithets applied to the Suwa deity include ''Nangū Daimyōjin'' (南宮大明神, "Daimyōjin of the Southern Shrine (''Nangū'')"), ''Hosshō Daimyōjin'' (法性大明神, "{{ill|Reality in Buddhism|bn|বৌদ্ধ বাস্তববাদ|es|Realidad en el budismo|hu|Valóság a buddhizmusban|qid=Q5551108|lt=Dharma-Nature}} Daimyōjin"), a combination of the two such as ''Nangū Hosshō Daimyōjin'' (南宮法性大明神), or ''Suwa Hosshō Kamishimo'' (or ''Jōge'') ''Daimyōjin'' (諏訪法性上下大明神, "Dharma-Nature Daimyōjin of the Upper and Lower Suwa [Shrines]").<ref>{{Cite Also shown are two of the four shrines that comprise [[Suwa-taisha|Suwa Taisha]] (''Kamisha Honmiya'' and ''Shimosha Akimiya'').]]
A number of explanations have been proposed for the origin of the term ''Nangū.'' One theory posits it to refer to the geographical location of the Upper Suwa Shrine, which is located ''southeast'' of Lake Suwa, at the ''southern'' half of Shinano Province, while another claims it to be derived from 'Minakatatomi' (南方刀美), one of the variant names for the deity, with ''minakata'' being apparently understood to mean "south(ern)" (cf. etymology of 'Takeminakata' above).<ref>Miyaji (1937). pp. 23-24.</ref> The term has also been interpreted to come from the medieval belief that the Suwa deity was the guardian of the ''south'' side of the [[Kyoto Imperial Palace|imperial palace]]<ref>Takei (1999). pp. 130, 142.</ref> or the [[Shinbutsu-shūgō|Shinto-Buddhist]] concept that the god is an enlightened being who [[Honji suijaku|manifested]] in our world, which in {{ill|Buddhist cosmology|blk|၃၁-ဘွုံႏ|bn|বৌদ্ধ মহাবিশ্বতত্ত্ব|cs|Buddhistická kosmologie|es|Cosmogonía budista|et|Budistlik kosmoloogia|fr|Cosmologie bouddhiste|hu|Buddhista kozmológia|id|Loka (Buddhisme)|it|Cosmologia buddista|ja|宇宙 (仏教)|ko|불교의 우주론|mk|Будистичка космологија|mr|बौद्ध विश्वउत्पत्तिशास्त्र|my|၃၁-ဘုံ|nl|Boeddhistische kosmos|no|Buddhistisk kosmologi|pl|Kosmologia buddyjska|pt|Cosmologia budista|ru|Буддийская космология|sh|Budistička kosmologija|sr|Будистичка космологија|ta|பௌத்த அண்டவியல்|vi|Vũ trụ học Phật giáo|qid=Q1308653|lt=Buddhist cosmology}} is the ''southern'' continent of {{ill|Jambudvīpa|awa|जम्बूद्वीप|bh|जंबूद्वीप|bn|জম্বুদ্বীপ|de|Jambudvipa|es|Yambuduipa|fa|جمبودویپ|fr|Jambudvipa|hi|जम्बूद्वीप|ja|閻浮提|ko|잠부드비파|ml|ജംബുദ്വീപ്|mn|Замбуутив|my|ဇမ္ဗူဒီပ (တောင်ကျွန်း)|ru|Джамбудвипа|si|ජම්බුද්වීප|sl|Džambudvipa|ta|நாவலந்தீவு|th|ชมพูทวีป|ur|جمبودویپہ|uz|Jambudvip|vi|Diêm phù đề|xal|Замбтив|zh|南贍部洲|zh_yue|南贍部洲|qid=Q1586228|lt=Jambudvīpa}}.<ref name="miyasakayusho" />

''Hosshō'', meanwhile, is believed to refer to the concept of the ''{{ill|Dharmakāya|az|Dharmakaya|bg|Дхармакая|bn|ধর্মকায়|cs|Dharmakája|et|Dharmakāya|fa|شاکیه مونی|fr|Dharmakāya|hu|Dharmakája|id|Dharmakāya|it|Dharmakāya|ja|法身|ko|법신|nl|Dharmakaya|no|Dharmakāya|pl|Dharmakaja|ru|Дхармакая|sk|Dharmakája|th|ธรรมกาย|tr|Dharmakāya|uk|Дгармакая|vi|Pháp thân|zh|法身|qid=Q1191427|lt=Dharmakāya}}'' (法性身, ''hosshōshin''), the formless, transcendent ultimate truth that is the source of all {{ill|Buddhahood|ar|بوذوية|az|Buddalıq|bcl|Pagka-Buddha|blk|ဗုဒ္ဓ|bn|বুদ্ধ (উপাধি)|fa|بوداساتوا|fr|Buddhatva|hi|बुद्धत्व|hu|Buddhaság|ia|Buddhitate|id|Kebuddhaan|ja|成仏|kbd|Будда|ko|부처|lmo|Buddhitaa|mag|बुद्धत्व|mr|बुद्धत्व|my|ဗုဒ္ဓ|pi|बुद्धत्ता|rki|ဗုဒ္ဓ|si|බුදුවරු|sv|Buddhaskap|ur|بدھتو|vi|Phật thành|zh|成佛|qid=Q56247062|lt=buddhas}}, which are its physical manifestations (''{{ill|Nirmāṇakāya|az|Nirmanakaya|bn|নির্মাণকায়|et|Nirmāṇakāya|fa|جسم لطیف|fr|Nirmāṇakāya|id|Nirmanakaya|ja|応身|ko|응신|nl|Nirmanakaya|no|Nirmāṇakāya|pl|Nirmanakaja|pt|Nirmāṇakaya|zh|應身|qid=Q3172811|lt=Nirmāṇakāya}}''). A certain medieval legend claims that the Suwa deity chose an eight-year-old boy to become his priest while declaring: "I have no (physical) body and so make this priest my [[Shintai|body]]".<ref name="miyasakayusho" /><ref>{{cite book |last1=Terada |first1=Shizuko |last2=Washio |first2=Tetsuta |title=諏訪明神―カミ信仰の原像 (Suwa Myōjin: Kami shinkō no genzō)|date=2010 |publisher=Iwata Shoin |page=116}}</ref>

==Mythology==

=== In imperial mythology ===

====Parentage====
Takeminakata is portrayed in both the ''Kojiki'' and the ''Sendai Kuji Hongi'' as a son of the god [[Ōkuninushi]], although the former does not include him in its genealogy of Ōkuninushi's children.<ref>Chamberlain (1882). [http://sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj033.htm Section XXVI.—The Deities the August Descendants of the Deity Master-of-the-Great-Land]</ref> The ''Kuji Hongi'' meanwhile identifies him as the son of Ōnamuchi (Ōkuninushi) with one of his wives, [[Nunakawahime]] of {{ill|Koshi Province (Japan)|de|Provinz Koshi (Japan)|es|Provincia de Koshi (Japón)|ff|Koshi Province (Japan)|fr|Province de Koshi (Japon)|ja|越国|ko|고시국|nl|Koshi (provincie)|pt|Província de Koshi|simple|Koshi Province (Japan)|zh|越國 (日本)|zh_min_nan|Kosi-kok|zh_yue|越國 (日本)|qid=Q1351611|lt=Koshi}}.<ref name="Hongi" /><ref>Chamberlain (1882). [http://sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj031.htm Section XXIV.—The Wooing of the Deity-of-Eight-Thousand-Spears.]</ref>

====Defeat by Takemikazuchi====
{{see also|Kuni-yuzuri}}

[[File:Shinpukuji-bon Kojiki (真福寺本古事記).png|thumb|401x401px|The passage concerning Takeminakata's appearance and defeat from the oldest extant manuscript of the ''[[Kojiki]]'', the Shinpukuji-bon (真福寺本, written 1371–1372)]]Takeminakata appears in both the ''Kojiki'' and the ''Kuji Hongi'' in the context of Ōkuninushi's "transfer of the land" (''kuni-yuzuri'') to the ''[[amatsukami]]'', the gods of the heavenly realm of [[Takamagahara]].<ref name="Chamberlain" /><ref name="KujiHongi03">{{cite web|title=先代舊事本紀卷第三|url=http://miko.org/~uraki/kuon/furu/text/sendaikuji/sendaikuji03.htm|website=私本 先代舊事本紀}}</ref>

When the heavenly deities, headed by the sun goddess [[Amaterasu]] and/or the [[Kotoamatsukami|primordial deity]] [[Takamimusubi]], sent [[Takemikazuchi]] and another messenger{{efn|[[Kamiumi#Birth of the gods|Ame-no-Torifune]] in the ''Kojiki'', [[Futsunushi]] in the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'' and the ''Kuji Hongi''}} to demand that Ōkuninushi relinquish his authority over the earthly realm of [[Ashihara no Nakatsukuni]] (the "Central Land of Reed-Plains") to Amaterasu's progeny, he told the messengers to consult his son [[Kotoshironushi-no-Mikoto|Kotoshironushi]], who immediately accepted their demands and advised his father to do likewise. Upon being asked if he had any other sons who ought to express their opinion, Ōkuninushi told the messengers that he had another son named Takeminakata.

<blockquote>As he was saying this, this same Takeminakata-no-Kami came bearing a tremendous boulder (千引之石, ''chibiki no iwa'', i.e. a boulder so large it would take a thousand men to pull) on his finger-tips and said:

"Who is it who has come to our land and is talking so furtively? Come, let us test our strength; I will first take your arm."

When [Takemikazuchi-no-Kami] allowed [Takeminakata-no-Kami] to take his arm, he changed it into a column of ice, then again changed it into a sword blade. At this, he (Takeminakata) was afraid and drew back.

Then [Takemikazuchi-no-Kami], in his turn, demanded [the right] to take hold of the arm of Takeminakata-no-Kami.

When he took it, it was like taking hold of a young reed; he grasped it and crushed it, throwing it aside. Immediately, he (Takeminakata) ran away.

They pursued him, and caught up with him by the {{ill|Lake Suwa|ar|بحيرة سوا|arz|بحيره سوا|ceb|Suwa Ko|de|Suwa-See|eo|Suŭa-Lago|es|Lago Suwa|et|Suwa järv|eu|Suwa aintzira|fa|دریاچه سووا|fr|Lac Suwa|id|Danau Suwa|ja|諏訪湖|ko|스와호|lt|Suva (ežeras)|mk|Сува (езеро)|my|ဆုဝကန်|nn|Suwasjøen|pl|Suwa (jezioro)|ro|Lacul Suwa|ru|Сува (озеро)|sr|Језеро Сува|th|ทะเลสาบซูวะ|tr|Suwa Gölü|vi|Hồ Suwa|zh|諏訪湖|zh_yue|諏訪湖|qid=Q1206692|lt=lake of Suwa}} in the {{ill|Shinano Province|ckb|پارێزگای شینانۆ|cs|Provincie Šinano|de|Provinz Shinano|eo|Provinco Ŝinano|es|Provincia de Shinano|fa|ولایت شینانو|fr|Province de Shinano|gl|Provincia de Shinano|hak|Shinano-koet|id|Provinsi Shinano|it|Shinano (provincia)|ja|信濃国|knc|Shinano Province|ko|시나노국|lt|Šinano žemė|ms|Wilayah Shinano|nl|Shinano (provincie)|pl|Prowincja Shinano|pt|Província de Shinano|ru|Синано (провинция)|simple|Shinano Province|sk|Šinano (provincia)|sr|Провинција Шинано|th|แคว้นชินาโนะ|tr|Shinano (vilayet)|uk|Провінція Сінано|zh|信濃國|zh_min_nan|Sinano-kok|zh_yue|信濃國|qid=Q289250|lt=land of Shinano}} (科野国州羽海). As they were about to kill him, Takeminakata-no-Kami said:

"Pray do not kill me. I will go to no other place. Also I will not disobey the commands of my father, Ōkuninushi-no-Kami, and will not disobey the words of the words of Yae-Kotoshironushi-no-Kami. I will yield this Central Land of the Reed Plains in accordance with the commands of the Heavenly Deities."<ref>Translation from {{cite book |last1=Philippi |first1=Donald L. |title=Kojiki |date=2015 |publisher=Princeton University Press |isbn=978-1400878000 |page=133 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QzjWCgAAQBAJ&pg=PA133}} Names (transcribed in {{ill|Old Japanese|ar|اللغة اليابانية القديمة|ast|Xaponés antiguu|azb|قدیمی ژاپون دیلی|ca|Japonès antic|de|Altjapanische Sprache|es|Japonés antiguo|fa|زبان ژاپنی باستان|id|Bahasa Jepang Kuno|it|Lingua giapponese antica|ja|上代日本語|ka|ძველი იაპონური ენა|ko|상대 일본어|ms|Bahasa Jepun Kuno|nn|Gamaljapansk|no|Gammeljapansk|ru|Старояпонский язык|simple|Old Japanese|su|Basa Jepang heubeul|tr|Eski Japonca|ur|قدیم جاپانی|vi|Tiếng Nhật thượng cổ|wikifunctions|Z1386|zh|上古日語|zh_yue|上古日語|qid=Q5736700|lt=Old Japanese}} in the original) have been changed into their modern equivalents.</ref></blockquote>

With Takeminakata's surrender, Ōkuninushi finally agreed to cede the land to the ''amatsukami'' and withdrew himself into the unseen spirit world.<ref name="Chamberlain" /><ref name="KujiHongi03" /><ref name="Hackin1932">{{cite book|author=J. Hackin|title=Asiatic Mythology: A Detailed Description and Explanation of the Mythologies of All the Great Nations of Asia|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HAZrFhvqnTkC&pg=PA395|year=1932|publisher=Asian Educational Services|isbn=978-81-206-0920-4|page=395}}</ref><ref name="Herbert2010">{{cite book|author=Jean Herbert|title=Shinto: At the Fountainhead of Japan|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Sg_JBQAAQBAJ&pg=PT437|date=18 October 2010|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-136-90376-2|page=437}}</ref><ref name="Ashkenazi2003">{{cite book|author=Michael Ashkenazi|title=Handbook of Japanese Mythology|url=https://archive.org/details/handbookofjapane0000ashk|url-access=registration|date=1 January 2003|publisher=ABC-CLIO|isbn=978-1-57607-467-1|pages=[https://archive.org/details/handbookofjapane0000ashk/page/267 267]–268}}</ref>

''{{ill|Florilegium|ast|Florilexu|de|Florilegium|es|Florilegio|eu|Florilegio|hu|Florilégium|id|Florilegium|it|Florilegium|lt|Florilegiumas|pl|Florilegium|pt|Florilégio|ru|Флорилегий|sh|Florilegij|sr|Флорилегији|qid=Q354326|lt=Florilegium}}'' that happened to omit the relevant passage. |text="(...) When he allowed him to take his hand, he changed it into a column of ice, and then changed it into a sword blade," <em>{{ill|Et cetera|ar|إلى آخره|bcl|Et cetera|bg|Et cetera|br|Et cætera|ca|Etcètera|de|Et cetera|es|Etcétera|fr|Et cetera|gan|幫助:等|gl|Etcétera|hy|Et cetera|ilo|Et cetera|it|Et cetera|lt|Et cetera|nl|Et cetera|nn|Et cetera|no|Et cetera|pt|Et cetera|ro|Etc.|ru|Et cetera|simple|Et cetera|sl|Et cetera|tr|Et cetera|uk|Et cetera|vi|Et cetera|zh|等等|zh_min_nan|Et cetera|qid=Q845653|lt=and so forth}}</em> (, ''unnun'').<br/>
"Upon arriving at the sea of Suwa in the land of Shinano, Takeminakata-no-Kami said, 'I will go to no other place. And I will not disobey the commands of my father Ōkuninushi-no-Kami, and will not disobey the words of the words of my elder brother Yae-Kotoshironushi-no-Kami. I will yield this Central Land of the Reed Plains in accordance with the commands of the Heavenly Deities.'"|source="The Matter of Suwa Shrine" (諏方社事, ''Suwa-sha no koto'')<ref name="Kojikijokan" /><ref name=":0" />}}

[[File:諏方社事 - Suwa-sha no Koto.png|left|thumb|Part of "The Matter of Suwa Shrine" (諏方社事, ''Suwa-sha no koto'') appended to the {{ill|Ōsu Kannon|arz|اوسو كانون|es|Templo Ōsu Kannon|eu|Ōsu Kannon|fr|Ōsu Kannon|ja|大須観音|ko|오스칸논|zh|大须观音|qid=Q3594052|lt=Shinpuku-ji}} ''Kojiki Jōkan-shō''. The omission of the passage recounting Takeminakata's defeat is marked with an  (''unnun'', "and so forth," "etc." - fourth column from left)]]
Based on textual affinities with the Urabe text of the ''Kojiki'', the ''Jōkan-shō'' is thought to have been authored by a member of the priestly [[Japanese clans#Sacerdotal clans|Urabe clan]] associated with the {{ill|Yoshida Shrine|arz|ضريح يوشيدا|az|Yoşida məbədi|de|Yoshida-Schrein|fa|معبد یوشیدا|fr|Yoshida-jinja|it|Santuario di Yoshida|ja|吉田神社|ko|요시다 신사|my|ယောရှိဒနတ်ကျောင်း|ru|Ёсида-дзиндзя|simple|Yoshida Shrine|zh|吉田神社|qid=Q713177|lt=Yoshida}} and [[Hirano Shrine|Hirano Shrines]] in Kyoto. Records indicate that during the medieval period, the ''Kuji Hongi'' was used by the [[Department of Divinities]] or ''Jingi-kan'' (in which many Urabe clan members occupied posts) as a go-to source for inquiries regarding the histories of various shrines across the country. It is also known that during his research for information regarding Suwa Shrine, Enchū sought the assistance of two Urabe clan members: Urabe Kanetoyo (卜部兼豊, of the Yoshida branch), then senior assistant director (神祇大輔, ''jingi taifu'') of the Jingi-kan, and Urabe Kanemae (卜部兼前, of the Hirano branch), either of whom may have been responsible for compiling "The Matter of Suwa Shrine." In other words, Enchu most likely did not (or could not) consult the ''Kuji Hongi'' itself, but was rather working with an extract provided by his Urabe contacts.<ref name=":0" />

Although he was not responsible for excising Takeminakata's surrender from the narrative himself, its absence from his source allowed Enchū to reimagine the ''Kuji Hongi'' narrative in a way that portrayed Takeminakata as a triumphant god who vowed to remain in Suwa of his own volition, consistent with the portrayal of the god of Suwa as an illustrious warrior deity in the ''Ekotoba''<nowiki/>'s later portions. Whereas in the original ''Kojiki'' and ''Kuji Hongi'' narrative, Takemikazuchi is said to have "changed [his arm] into a column of ice, then again changed it into a sword blade" (取成立氷亦取成劍刃) after having it grasped by Takeminakata, Enchū - taking advantage of the ambiguous syntax of the original {{ill|Classical Chinese|ar|اللغة الصينية الكلاسيكية|ast|Chinu clásicu|az|Klassik Çin dili|azb|قدیم چین دیلی|be|Вэньянь|bg|Класически китайски език|bn|শাস্ত্রীয় চীনাভাষা|ca|Xinès clàssic|cdo|Ùng-ngiòng-ùng|cs|Klasická čínština|de|Klassisches Chinesisch|el|Κλασική κινεζική γλώσσα|eo|Klasika ĉina lingvo|es|Chino clásico|et|Vanahiina kirjakeel|eu|Txinera klasiko|fa|زبان چینی کلاسیک|fr|Chinois classique|gan|文言文|gl|Chinés clásico|he|סינית קלאסית|hi|शास्त्रीय चीनी भाषा|hr|Literarni kineski|hu|Klasszikus kínai nyelv|id|Bahasa Tionghoa Klasik|ilo|Klasiko nga Insik|it|Cinese classico|ja|漢文|kk|Вэньянь|ko|한문|ms|Bahasa Cina Klasik|nl|Klassiek Chinees|nn|Wenyan|no|Wenyan|pl|Klasyczny język chiński|pt|Chinês clássico|ru|Классический китайский язык|sat|ᱠᱞᱟᱥᱤᱠᱟᱞ ᱪᱟᱭᱱᱤᱡᱽ|sc|Tzinesu classicu|sh|Klasični kineski jezik|simple|Classical Chinese|sk|Klasická čínština|sr|Класични кинески језик|sv|Klassisk kinesiska|tr|Klasik Çince|uk|Класична китайська мова|vi|Văn ngôn|wikifunctions|Z1152|wuu|文言文|zh|文言文|zh_classical|文言|zh_min_nan|Hàn-bûn|zh_yue|文言|qid=Q37041|lt=Classical Chinese}} text - chooses to read the text such that ''Takeminakata'' is now said to magically materialize ice and a sword as a display of his power to Takemikazuchi (即氷ヲ成立、又劍ヲ取成, "he (Takeminakata) caused ice to appear, and then he manifested a sword").<ref name=":0" />

have originally been specific to the imperial court - see '[[Takeminakata#Analysis|Analysis]]' below) into Suwa itself - where other myths concerning the Suwa deity were in circulation - for the first time.<ref name="Maeda2023">Maeda (2023). pp. 16-30.</ref>

Ryōtarō Maeda (2023), based on a study of surviving manuscripts of the text, postulates that the ''Ekotoba'' was only introduced to Suwa itself no earlier than the 17th century, where it gradually gained acceptance among the priestly families of Suwa Shrine, who produced a number of copies of it. Soon, the influence of the ''Ekotoba'' can be seen in a number of texts from the area: a text penned by the ''{{ill|Hatamoto|ar|هاتاموتو (لقب)|bg|Хатамото|ca|Hatamoto|cs|Hatamoto|de|Hatamoto|es|Hatamoto|fa|هاتاموتو|fr|Hatamoto|id|Hatamoto|it|Hatamoto|ja|旗本|ko|하타모토|pl|Hatamoto|pt|Hatamoto|ru|Хатамото|tr|Hatamoto|uk|Хатамото|zh|旗本|qid=Q572662|lt=Hatamoto}}'' [[:ja:諏訪盛條|Suwa Morieda]] (1646-1695), the younger brother of [[Suwa Domain#Suwa Tadaharu|Suwa Tadaharu]], the third ''daimyō'' of {{ill|Suwa Domain|fa|قلمرو سووا|fr|Domaine de Suwa|id|Wilayah Suwa|ja|諏訪藩|pt|Domínio de Suwa|ru|Сува (княжество)|zh|諏訪藩|qid=Q3034531|lt=Takashima Domain}} in 1684 titled ''Shinshu Suwa Daimyōjin Engi'' (信州諏方大明神縁起, "The Origin Story of Suwa Daimyōjin of Shinano Province"), for instance, features the reinterpreted ''kuni-yuzuri'' myth, which Morieda then interprets in a {{ill|Edo neo-Confucianism|ar|كونفوشية إيدو الجديدة|fa|نئوکنفوسیوس‌گرایی ادو|ko|일본 주자학|pt|Shushi-Gaku|th|ลัทธิขงจื่อใหม่แบบเอโดะ|zh|日本朱子学|qid=Q5340141|lt=Neo-Confucian}} light as a meritorious act of filial piety comparable to {{ill|Taibo|de|Wu Tai Bo|fr|Taibo de Wu|id|Taibo|ja|太伯・虞仲|ko|오 태백|pt|Taibo|th|อู๋ไท่ปั๋ว|ur|ٹیبو|vi|Ngô Thái Bá|wuu|泰伯|zh|泰伯|zh_classical|太伯|qid=Q1010535|lt=Taibo}}'s renunciation of the throne of {{ill|Predynastic Zhou|ar|ولاية تشو ما قبل السلالة|ckb|ویلایەتی ژۆو (پێش ئیمپراتۆریەت)|es|Zhou predinástico|fa|ژو پیش‌دودمان|fr|Zhou Prédynastiques|id|Pra-Dinasti Zhou|sv|Zhou (predynastisk)|zh|周國|qid=Q16924982|lt=Zhou}}.<ref name="Maeda2023"/>

[But] he repented and eventually ceded the Central Land to the Heavenly Grandson. He departed, arriving at the sea of Suwa in the land of Shinano.<br/>

[[File:Lake Suwa 20131231 - panoramio (cropped).jpg|thumb|{{ill|Lake Suwa|ar|بحيرة سوا|arz|بحيره سوا|ceb|Suwa Ko|de|Suwa-See|eo|Suŭa-Lago|es|Lago Suwa|et|Suwa järv|eu|Suwa aintzira|fa|دریاچه سووا|fr|Lac Suwa|id|Danau Suwa|ja|諏訪湖|ko|스와호|lt|Suva (ežeras)|mk|Сува (езеро)|my|ဆုဝကန်|nn|Suwasjøen|pl|Suwa (jezioro)|ro|Lacul Suwa|ru|Сува (озеро)|sr|Језеро Сува|th|ทะเลสาบซูวะ|tr|Suwa Gölü|vi|Hồ Suwa|zh|諏訪湖|zh_yue|諏訪湖|qid=Q1206692|lt=Lake Suwa}}]]
As late as the 19th century (when awareness of the ''Kojiki''<nowiki/>'s contents had become much more widespread due to the efforts of ''{{ill|Kokugaku|ar|كوكوجاكو|ast|Kokugaku|bg|Кокугаку|ca|Kokugaku|de|Kokugaku|es|Kokugaku|fa|کوکوگاکو|fi|Kokugaku|fr|Kokugaku|gl|Kokugaku|hu|Kokugaku|id|Kokugaku|it|Kokugaku|ja|国学|ko|국학 (일본사)|ms|Kokugaku|pt|Kokugaku|ru|Кокугаку|sah|Кокугаку|tr|Kokugaku|uk|Кокуґаку|zh|國學 (日本)|qid=Q855159|lt=Kokugaku}}'' scholars), this positive reinterpretation of the ''kuni-yuzuri'' narrative continued to be found within Suwa: a mid-19th century genealogical chart of Takeminakata issued by the Upper Shrine for instance quotes the above passage from the ''Shinshu Suwa Daimyōjin Engi''.<ref>Maeda (2023). p. 23.</ref> A document submitted in 1834 to the Commissioner of Shrines and Temples (''[[Jisha-bugyō]]'') by the Lower Shrine's Momoi clan (桃井氏) of priests relates the following:

{{Blockquote
|text=When the two deities of Kashima and Katori came down to the land of Izumo at the command of the heavenly deities, he [Takeminakata] fought for his land bearing a heavy rock on his fingertips and engaged in a test of strength. <em>He also took up a sword and exhibited valor.</em> When he, leading [an army of] divine soldiers, arrived at the sea of Suwa in the land of Shinano, he offered up the Central Land of the Reed Plains to the Heavenly Grandson. As his divine father had ceded the land, he made a vow to never go to another place. This is the account of this shrine's establishment.<ref>Maeda (2023). p. 24.</ref>}}

A third text found in the archives of the Upper Shrine's Moriya (守矢氏) priestly clan titled "The Origin of Suwa Daimyōjin" (諏訪大明神由来, ''Suwa Daimyōjin yurai'') features Takeminakata striking fear into Futsunushi and Takemikazuchi after displaying his power to them, only agreeing to cede Ashihara no Nakatsukuni after he was convinced by their reasoning. The three then go to Suwa, where they defeat the local deity [[Moriya|Moriya]] (see below).<ref>Maeda (2023). p. 30.</ref>

===== Other versions =====
Similar attempts at retelling or reinterpreting the myth in a more positive way are found in other texts. In one version, for instance, Takeminakata is portrayed as going to Suwa not so much to flee from Takemikazuchi but to pacify it under the orders of his father Ōkuninushi.<ref>Miyaji (1937). pp. 48-49.</ref>

A variant found in a commentary on the ''Nihon Shoki'' penned by a 15th-century monk named Shun'yu (春瑜), the ''Nihon Shoki Shikenmon'' (日本書紀私見聞), claims 'Suwa Daimyōjin' (諏防大明神) to be the third son of the deity [[:ja:山王権現|Sannō Gongen]], the guardian deity of {{ill|Mount Hiei|ar|جبل هيه|arz|جبل هيه|ast|Monte Hiei|az|Hiey dağı|ca|Mont Hiei|ceb|Hiei-zan|cs|Hiei|de|Hiei-zan|es|Monte Hiei|eu|Hiei mendia|fa|کوه هیئی|fi|Hieivuori|fr|Mont Hiei|he|הר היאיי|hu|Hiei-hegy|id|Gunung Hiei|it|Monte Hiei|ja|比叡山|ko|히에이산|lld|Mont Hiei|my|ဟိအဲတောင်|nl|Hiei (berg)|pag|Palandey na Hiei|pl|Hiei (góra)|ro|Hiei|ru|Хиэй|simple|Mount Hiei|tr|Hiei Dağı|uk|Гора Хієй|vi|Núi Hiei|wuu|比叡山|zh|比叡山|zh_yue|比叡山|qid=Q748040|lt=Mount Hiei}}. After engaging in a failed rebellion against Amaterasu, the deity surrendered and settled down in the land of Shinano.<ref>Miyaji (1937). pp. 47.</ref>

Local legends from within Nagano Prefecture claim Takeminakata to have passed or stayed in various places within the region during his escape. A local legend in {{ill|Shimoina District, Nagano|de|Shimoina-gun|fa|ناحیه شیموینا، ناگانو|fi|Shimo-Inan piirikunta|fr|District de Shimoina|it|Distretto di Shimoina|ja|下伊那郡|ko|시모이나군|pl|Powiat Shimoina|uk|Повіт Сімо-Іна|zh|下伊那郡|qid=Q726999|lt=Shimoina District}} (located south of Suwa) for instance claims that Takemikazuchi caught up with the fleeing Takeminakata in the modern village of {{ill|Toyooka, Nagano|ceb|Toyooka-mura|es|Toyooka (Nagano)|fa|تویوئوکا، ناگانو|fi|Toyooka (Nagano)|fr|Toyooka (Nagano)|hy|Տոյոոկա (գյուղ)|it|Toyooka (Nagano)|ja|豊丘村|ko|도요오카촌|pl|Toyooka (Nagano)|ru|Тоёока (село)|th|โทโยโอกะ (จังหวัดนางาโนะ)|tl|Toyooka, Nagano|tr|Toyooka, Nagano|uk|Тойоока (Наґано)|ur|ٹویوکا، ناگانو|uz|Toyooka (Nagano)|zh|豐丘村 (日本)|qid=Q44545|lt=Toyooka}}, where they agreed to an armistice and left imprints of their hands on a rock as a sign of their agreement. The rock, bearing the gods' supposed handprints (''tegata''), is found in Otegata Shrine (御手形神社) in Toyooka.<ref>{{cite web |title=国護りと天孫降臨の神話ー御手形石ー |url=http://www.ja-mis.iijan.or.jp/gotominami/hometown/2016/11/post_140.php |website=JA Minami Shinshu official website}}</ref> After Takemikazuchi's departure, Takeminakata temporarily resided in the neighboring village of {{ill|Ōshika, Nagano|ceb|Ōshika-mura|es|Ōshika|fa|اوشیکا، ناگانو|fi|Ōshika|fr|Ōshika|hy|Օսիկա (գյուղ)|it|Ōshika|ja|大鹿村|ko|오시카촌|my|အိုးရှိခရွာ၊ နဂနို|pl|Ōshika|pt|Ōshika|ru|Осика (село)|tl|Ōshika, Nagano|tr|Ōshika|uk|Осіка (Наґано)|ur|اوشیکا، ناگانو|uz|Ōshika (Nagano)|zh|大鹿村|qid=Q1203751|lt=Ōshika}}, where he discovered hot springs of saltwater while hunting for deer.<ref>{{cite web |title=塩水の湧泉から採取される大鹿村の山塩の謎 |url=http://www.iijan.or.jp/oishii/area/post-1085.php |website=長野県のおいしい食べ方 |date=June 23, 2009 |publisher=JA Nagano Chuoukai}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Matsumae |first1=Takashi |title=日本神話の形成 (Nihon shinwa no keisei) |publisher=Hanawa Shobō|page=431}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |editor1-last=Satō|editor1-first=Shigenao|title=南信伊那史料 巻之下 (Nanshin Ina Shiryō, vol. 02)|date=1901|page=55 |url=http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/765237/30}}</ref>

=== Other myths ===

====Entry into Suwa====
{{see also|Moreya}}

[[File:Fujishima Shrine (Nakasu, Suwa) - 藤島社（諏訪市中洲）- 2.jpg|thumb|353x353px|Fujishima Shrine (藤島社) in [[:en:Suwa City|Suwa City]]. It is one of two 'Fujishima Shrines' associated with Suwa Myōjin's battle against Moriya; the other is located in {{ill|Okaya, Nagano|ar|أوكايا (ناغانو)|azb|اوکایا، ناقانو|ce|Окая|ceb|Okaya (lungsod sa Hapon)|de|Okaya|es|Okaya (Nagano)|fa|اوکایا|fi|Okaya|fr|Okaya (Nagano)|gl|Okaya|hy|Օկայա|id|Okaya, Nagano|it|Okaya|ja|岡谷市|ko|오카야시|mzn|اوکایا، ناگانو|nl|Okaya|no|Okaya|pl|Okaya|pt|Okaya|ro|Okaya|ru|Окая|sv|Okaya|tg|Окая|th|โอกายะ|tl|Okaya, Nagano|tr|Okaya|tt|Окая|uk|Окая (Наґано)|ur|اوکایا، ناگانو|uz|Okaya (Nagano)|vi|Okaya, Nagano|war|Okaya, Nagano|zh|岡谷市|zh_classical|岡谷市|zh_min_nan|Okaya-chhī|zh_yue|岡谷|qid=Q838672|lt=the city of Okaya}} by the Tenryū River.]]
A myth from the Suwa area portrays Suwa Myōjin as being opposed during his advent by the local god [[Moriya|Moriya]] (Moreya).

A document supposedly submitted to the {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|azb|کاماکورا شوگونلوغو|be|Сёгунат Камакура|ca|Shogunat Kamakura|ckb|زنجیرە شۆگنی کاماکورا|cs|Šógunát Kamakura|de|Kamakura-Shōgunat|el|Σογκουνάτο Καμακούρα|es|Shogunato Kamakura|eu|Kamakura shogunerria|fa|شوگون‌سالاری کاماکورا|fi|Kamakura-shōgunaatti|fr|Shogunat de Kamakura|hak|Kamakura mok-fú|he|שוגונות קמקורה|hu|Kamakura-bakufu|id|Keshogunan Kamakura|it|Shogunato Kamakura|ja|鎌倉幕府|ko|가마쿠라 막부|ms|Kesyogunan Kamakura|nl|Kamakura-shogunaat|no|Kamakura-shōgunatet|pl|Kamakura (okres)|pt|Xogunato Kamakura|ru|Сёгунат Камакура|simple|Kamakura shogunate|sr|Камакура шогунат|th|รัฐบาลโชกุนคามากูระ|tr|Kamakura şogunluğu|uk|Сьоґунат Камакура|vi|Mạc phủ Kamakura|zh|镰仓幕府|zh_min_nan|Kamakura bō͘-hú|zh_yue|鎌倉幕府|qid=Q736839|lt=Kamakura shogunate}} in 1249 by Suwa Nobushige, then high priest or ''Ōhōri'' (大祝) of the Upper Shrine of Suwa, known as the ''Suwa Nobushige Gejō'' (諏訪信重解状 "The Petition of Suwa Nobushige"), relates a story from "the ancient customs" (舊貫) that the Suwa deity came down from heaven in order to take possession of the land of 'Moriya Daijin' (守屋大臣). The conflict between the two escalated into a battle, but as no winner could be declared, the two finally compete in a {{ill|Tug of war|af|Toutrek|ang|Tygelwīg|ar|شد الحبل|as|ৰছী টনা খেল|bn|রশি টানা|br|Sach-fun|ca|Joc d'estirar la corda|chr|ᏍᏕᏯᏓ ᎬᏘ ᏓᎾᏓᏌᏁᏍᎬ|cs|Přetahování lanem|da|Tovtrækning|de|Tauziehen|dv|ވާ ދެމުން|el|Διελκυστίνδα|eo|Ŝnurtira lukto|es|Juego de la soga|et|Köievedu|eu|Sokatira|fa|طناب‌کشی|fi|Köydenveto|fr|Tir à la corde|gl|Tiro de corda|hak|Pâng-sok-é|he|משיכת חבל|hi|रस्साकशी|hr|Potezanje konopa|hu|Kötélhúzás|hy|Պարանձգություն|hyw|Պարան քաշելու խաղ|id|Tarik tambang|is|Reiptog|it|Tiro alla fune|ja|綱引き|kk|Арқан тарту|km|ល្បែងទាញព្រ័ត្រ|kn|ಟಗ್ ಆಫ್ ವಾರ್|ko|줄다리기|ky|Аркан тартыш|la|Tractus funis|lt|Virvės traukimas|lv|Virves vilkšana|ml|വടംവലി|ms|Tarik tali|nds|Tautrecken|nl|Touwtrekken|nn|Dragkamp|no|Tautrekking|pa|ਰੱਸਾ ਕਸ਼ੀ|pl|Przeciąganie liny|pt|Cabo de guerra|ro|Lupta cu odgonul|ru|Перетягивание каната|scn|Tirata dâ corda|sh|Potezanje konopca|simple|Tug of war|sk|Preťahovanie lanom|sr|Надвлачење конопца|sv|Dragkamp|sw|Kuvuta kamba|ta|கயிறு இழுத்தல்|th|ชักเย่อ|tr|Halat çekme|uk|Перетягування канату|uz|Arqon tortish oʻyini|vi|Kéo co|wuu|拉绳|zh|拔河|zh_yue|扯大纜|qid=Q102843|lt=Tug of war}} using hooks (''kagi''): Suwa Myōjin, using a hook made out of the [[wisteria]] plant (藤鎰), emerges victorious against Moriya, who used an iron hook (鐵鎰). After his victory, the god built his dwelling (what would become the Upper Shrine) in Moriya's land and planted the wisteria hook, which became a grove known as the 'Forest of Fujisuwa' (藤諏訪之森 ''Fujisuwa no mori'').{{efn|「一 守屋山麓御垂跡事<br>
右謹檢舊貫、當砌昔者守屋大臣之所領也、大神天降御之刻、大臣者奉禦明神之居住、勵制止之方法、明神者廻可爲御敷地之祕計、或致諍論、或及合戰之處、兩方難決雌雄、爰明神者持藤鎰、大臣者以鐵鎰、懸此所引之、明神即以藤鎰令勝得軍陣之諍論給、而間令追罰守屋大臣、卜居所當社以來、遙送數百歲星霜、久施我神之稱譽天下給、應跡之方々是新哉、明神以彼藤鎰自令植當社之前給、藤榮枝葉號藤諏訪之森、毎年二ヶ度御神事勤之、自尓以來以當郡名諏方、爰下宮者當社依夫婦之契約示姫大明神之名、然而當大明神、若不令追出守屋給者、爭兩者卜居御哉、自天降之元初爲本宮之條炳焉者哉、」}}<ref name="GejoEkotoba">Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai, ed. (1995). pp. 811–814.</ref><ref name="Miyasaka9293">Miyasaka (1992). pp. 92-93.</ref><ref name="fukudachusei">Fukuda; Nihonmatsu; Tokuda, eds. (2015). pp. 121-124.</ref> Whereas the ''Kojiki'' portrays Takeminakata as an earthly god defeated by a deity from heaven, this myth notably features the opposite scenario, in which the deity of Suwa descends from heaven and conquers the land below.

The ''Suwa Daimyōjin Ekotoba'' relates a variant of this myth as an origin story of Fujishima Shrine (藤島社) in {{ill|Suwa, Nagano|ar|سوا (ناغانو)|azb|سووا، ناقانو|ce|Сува (гӀала)|ceb|Suwa (lungsod)|de|Suwa (Nagano)|es|Suwa (Nagano)|fa|سووا، ناگانو|fi|Suwa|fr|Suwa (Nagano)|gl|Suwa|hy|Սուվա (քաղաք)|id|Suwa, Nagano|it|Suwa|ja|諏訪市|ko|스와시|mzn|سووا، ناگانو|nl|Suwa|pl|Suwa (miasto)|pt|Suwa (Nagano)|ro|Suwa|ru|Сува (город)|sv|Suwa, Nagano|tg|Сува|th|ซูวะ|tl|Suwa, Nagano|tr|Suwa|tt|Сува (шәһәр)|uk|Сува (Наґано)|ur|سووا، ناگانو|uz|Suva (Nagano)|vi|Suwa, Nagano|war|Suwa, Nagano|zh|諏訪市|zh_classical|諏訪市|zh_min_nan|Suwa-chhī|zh_yue|諏訪|qid=Q846338|lt=Suwa City}}, one of the Upper Shrine's [[Setsumatsusha|auxiliary shrines]] where its yearly rice-planting ceremony is traditionally held.<ref name="fukudachusei"/><ref name="Suwashishi681">Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai, ed. (1995). pp. 681-683.</ref><ref>Miyasaka (1992). pp. 88-91.</ref> In this version, the deity of Fujishima Shrine (藤島の明神 ''Fujishima no Myōjin'') - usually equated with Suwa Myōjin - defeats "Moriya the evil outlaw" (洩矢の惡賊, ''Moriya no akuzoku'') with a wisteria branch:

{{Quote|Regarding the god of Fujishima [Shrine] (藤島の明神, ''Fujishima no Myōjin''): when the revered deity (尊神, ''sonjin'', i.e. Suwa Daimyōjin) [[Honji suijaku|manifested]] long ago, Moriya the evil outlaw (洩矢の惡賊, ''Moriya no akuzoku''), seeking to hinder him, took up an iron ring (鐵輪) to fight him, but the [Fujishima] deity picked up a wisteria branch and defeated [Moriya]. Finally, he brought down heresy (邪輪, ''jarin'', lit. "ring/wheel/circle of evil") and held up {{ill|Dharma (Buddhism)|blk|ဓမ္မ|bo|ཆོས།|br|Dharma (boudaegezh)|id|Dhamma|it|Dharma (buddismo)|ja|法 (仏教)|ko|다르마 (불교)|mn|Бурхны ном|my|ဓမ္မ|pt|Darma (budismo)|simple|Dharma (Buddhism)|sl|Dharma|th|พระธรรม (ศาสนาพุทธ)|tr|Dharma (Budizm)|zh|法 (佛教)|qid=Q9241518|lt=the true Dharma}} (正法, ''shōbō''). When the god pronounced a vow and threw the wisteria branch away, immediately it took root [in the ground], its branches and leaves flourishing in abundance, and [sprouted] beautiful blossoms, leaving behind a marker of the battleground for posterity. The Fujishima deity is named thus for this reason.{{efn|「抑コノ藤嶋ノ明神ト申ハ、尊神垂迹ノ昔、洩矢ノ惡賊神居ヲサマタケントセシ時、洩矢ハ鐵輪ヲ持シテアラソヒ、明神ハ藤枝ヲトリテ是ヲ伏シ給フ。ツイニ邪輪ヲ降シテ正法ヲ興ス。 明神誓ヲ發テ、藤枝ヲナケ給シカハ、則根ヲサシテ枝葉ヲサカヘ、花蘂アサヤカニシテ、戰場ノシルシヲ萬代ニ殘ス。藤嶋ノ明神ト号スル此ユヘナリ。」}}<ref>Kanai (1982). p. 262.</ref><ref>Hanawa, ed. (1914). p. 530.</ref>}}
[[File:Fujishima Shrine - 藤島神社 (川岸天竜河畔諏訪明神入諏伝説の地).jpg|alt=|thumb|Fujishima Shrine (藤島神社) in {{ill|Okaya, Nagano|ar|أوكايا (ناغانو)|azb|اوکایا، ناقانو|ce|Окая|ceb|Okaya (lungsod sa Hapon)|de|Okaya|es|Okaya (Nagano)|fa|اوکایا|fi|Okaya|fr|Okaya (Nagano)|gl|Okaya|hy|Օկայա|id|Okaya, Nagano|it|Okaya|ja|岡谷市|ko|오카야시|mzn|اوکایا، ناگانو|nl|Okaya|no|Okaya|pl|Okaya|pt|Okaya|ro|Okaya|ru|Окая|sv|Okaya|tg|Окая|th|โอกายะ|tl|Okaya, Nagano|tr|Okaya|tt|Окая|uk|Окая (Наґано)|ur|اوکایا، ناگانو|uz|Okaya (Nagano)|vi|Okaya, Nagano|war|Okaya, Nagano|zh|岡谷市|zh_classical|岡谷市|zh_min_nan|Okaya-chhī|zh_yue|岡谷|qid=Q838672|lt=Okaya}}]]
Two extant medieval genealogies of the Suwa (Miwa) clan also begin by recounting the legend of a battle between the Suwa deity, accompanied by the first high priest of the Upper Shrine, and 'Moriya' (守屋) during the reign of {{ill|Emperor Yōmei|ar|الإمبراطور يومي|arz|الامبراطور يومى|azb|یومی (ایمپیراتور)|bn|সম্রাট ইওমি|ckb|ئیمپراتۆر یۆمێی|cs|Jómei|de|Yōmei|es|Yōmei Tennō|fa|امپراتور یومی|fi|Yōmei|fr|Yōmei|id|Kaisar Yōmei|it|Yōmei|ja|用明天皇|ka|იომეი|ko|요메이 천황|nl|Yomei|pl|Yōmei|pt|Yomei|ru|Император Ёмэй|sh|Car Yōmei|simple|Emperor Yōmei|sl|Cesar Jomei|sv|Yomei|th|จักรพรรดิโยเม|tl|Emperador Yōmei|tr|Yōmei (imparator)|uk|Імператор Йомей|uz|Imperator Yōmei|vi|Thiên hoàng Yōmei|yo|Emperor Yōmei|zh|用明天皇|zh_min_nan|Yômei Thian-hông|zh_yue|用明天皇|qid=Q349281|lt=Emperor Yōmei}} (585-587).<ref>Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai, ed. (1995). p. 690.</ref>

In later versions of this story which combine it with the ''kuni-yuzuri'' myth, Moriya opposes Takeminakata after the latter had fled from Izumo. After being defeated, Moriya swears fealty to Takeminakata and becomes a faithful ally.<ref name="Imai1960">Imai (1960). pp. 3-15.</ref><ref name="Imai1976">Imai (1976). p. 41.</ref> Moriya is reckoned as the divine ancestor of the Moriya (守矢) clan, one of the former priestly lineages of the Upper Shrine.<ref name="Moriya">Moriya, Sanae (2017). ''守矢神長家のお話し (Moriya Jinchōke no ohanashi),'' in {{cite book |editor=Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum |title=神長官守矢史料館のしおり (Jinchōkan Moriya Shiryōkan no shiori)|pages=2–3|publisher=Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum|edition=3rd}}</ref>

Apart from Moriya, a few scattered local legends make reference to other deities who either submitted to the Suwa deity or refused to do so. One such god that is said to have opposed Suwa Myōjin and his new ally Moriya in local folklore was Yatsukao-no-Mikoto (矢塚男命), also known as Ganigawara (蟹河原長者 ''Ganigawara-chōja'').<ref name="Kobuzoku79">Kobuzoku Kenkyūkai, ed. (2017b). p 79.</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=蟹河原 （茅野市ちの横内）|url=http://tateshina-times.jp/?p=7866|website=たてしなの時間|publisher=蓼科企画}}</ref><ref name="suwashi-keizu">''Shinano-no-kuni Kansha Suwa-jinja Jinchōkan Moriya-ke Ryaku-keizu'' (信濃國官社諏訪神社神長官守矢家略系圖), in {{cite book|author1=Nobukawa, Kazuhiko (延川和彦)|author2=Iida, Kotaro (飯田好太郎)|title=諏訪氏系図 続編 (Suwa-shi Keizu, Zokuhen)|date=1921|page=19|url=http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/927368/21}}</ref>

The story relates that Ganigawara, a horse breeder who wielded great authority in the region, held Moriya in contempt for surrendering to Takeminakata and had messengers publicly harass him by calling him a coward. When Ganigawara's servants began to resort to violence by shooting arrows in Takeminakata's newly built house, Takeminakata retaliated by invading Ganigawara's turf. Mortally wounded by an arrow in the ensuing battle, Ganigawara begs forgiveness from Moriya and entrusts his youngest daughter to Takeminakata, who gives her in marriage to the god Taokihooi-no-Mikoto (手置帆負命) a.k.a. Hikosachi-no-Kami (彦狭知神),{{efn|Both Taokihooi and Hikosachi - identified as two distinct individuals - appear in the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]''<ref>{{cite wikisource |title=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |wslink=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |chapter=Book II |last=Aston |first=William George |authorlink=William George Aston |year=1896 |publisher=Kegan Paul, Trench, Trübner & Co. |location=London |page=81 |scan=Page:Nihongi_by_Aston.djvu/112 |quote=Thereupon Ta-oki-ho-ohi no Kami, ancestor of the Imbe of the Land of Kii, was appointed hatter, Hiko-sachi no Kami was made shield-maker ...}}</ref><ref>{{cite wikisource |wslink=zh:日本書紀 |chapter=卷第二 |title=日本書紀 |quote=既以紀伊國忌部遠祖手置帆負神、定爲作笠者。狹知神、爲作盾者。}}</ref> and the ''[[Kogo Shūi]]''<ref>{{cite wikisource |wslink=zh:古語拾遺 |title=古語拾遺 |quote=手置帆負命。<sub>讚岐國忌部祖也。</sub>產狹知命。<sub>紀伊國忌部祖也。</sub>}}</ref> as ancestors of the Inbe clan (忌部氏).}} who was injured by Ganigawara's messengers as he was keeping watch over Takeminakata's abode.<ref>Imai (1960). pp. 42-49.</ref><ref>Imai (1976). pp. 46-51.</ref>

In another legend, a god named Takei-Ōtomonushi (武居大伴主神 or 武居大友主神) swore allegiance to Takeminakata and became the ancestor of a line of priests in the Lower Shrine known as the ''Takeihōri'' (武居祝).<ref>Miyasaka (1987). p. 22.</ref><ref name="Kobuzoku79" /> Yet another story relates that the Suwa deity forbade the goddess of Sakinomiya Shrine (先宮神社) in Owa, {{ill|Suwa, Nagano|ar|سوا (ناغانو)|azb|سووا، ناقانو|ce|Сува (гӀала)|ceb|Suwa (lungsod)|de|Suwa (Nagano)|es|Suwa (Nagano)|fa|سووا، ناگانو|fi|Suwa|fr|Suwa (Nagano)|gl|Suwa|hy|Սուվա (քաղաք)|id|Suwa, Nagano|it|Suwa|ja|諏訪市|ko|스와시|mzn|سووا، ناگانو|nl|Suwa|pl|Suwa (miasto)|pt|Suwa (Nagano)|ro|Suwa|ru|Сува (город)|sv|Suwa, Nagano|tg|Сува|th|ซูวะ|tl|Suwa, Nagano|tr|Suwa|tt|Сува (шәһәр)|uk|Сува (Наґано)|ur|سووا، ناگانو|uz|Suva (Nagano)|vi|Suwa, Nagano|war|Suwa, Nagano|zh|諏訪市|zh_classical|諏訪市|zh_min_nan|Suwa-chhī|zh_yue|諏訪|qid=Q846338|lt=Suwa City}} from building a bridge over the creek before her shrine as punishment for her refusal to submit to him.<ref name="Kobuzoku79" /><ref>{{cite web |title=先宮神社 |url=https://www.jinriki.info/kaidolist/koshukaido/kamisuwa_shimosuwa/sakinomiyajinja.html |website=人力（じんりき）- 旧街道ウォーキング}}</ref>

====The ''Ōhōri''====
{{see also|Suwa clan}}

[[File:Japanese crest Suwa Kajinoha(White background).svg|thumb|left|The crest (''[[:en:Kamon (crest)|kamon]]'') of the [[Suwa clan]], which is also used by the Upper Shrine of Suwa as its emblem.]]
Before the abolition of the Suwa Grand Shrine's traditional priestly offices during the {{ill|Meiji era|ar|فترة مييجي|ast|Dómina Meiji|az|Meydzi dövrü|azb|مئی‌جی دؤورو|be|Перыяд Мэйдзі|bn|মেইজি যুগ|bo|མེའི་ཇིའི་དུས་དུས་མཚམས།|ca|Era Meiji|ceb|Panahon sa Meiji|cs|Období Meidži|da|Meiji-perioden|de|Meiji-Zeit|el|Μεϊτζί (περίοδος)|es|Era Meiji|et|Meiji periood|eu|Meiji Aroa|fa|دوره میجی|fi|Meiji-kausi|fr|Ère Meiji|gl|Período Meiji|he|תקופת מייג'י|hr|Meiji (razdoblje)|ht|Epòk Meiji|hu|Meidzsi-kor|id|Zaman Meiji|io|Ero Meiji|is|Meiji-tímabilið|it|Periodo Meiji|ja|明治|ka|მეიძის ეპოქა|kbp|Mejii wɛɛ yaa alɩwaatʊ|kk|Мэйдзи дәуірі|ko|메이지 시대|la|Aetas Meiji|lt|Meidži laikotarpis|lv|Meidzi periods|mk|Меиџи (период)|mn|Мэйжийн эрин|ms|Zaman Meiji|nl|Meijiperiode|nn|Meiji|no|Meiji-perioden|pl|Meiji (okres)|pt|Era Meiji|ro|Perioada Meiji|ru|Мэйдзи|simple|Meiji period|sk|Obdobie Meidži|sq|Periudha Meixhi|sr|Меиџи период|sv|Meijiperioden|ta|மெய்சி காலம்|th|ยุคเมจิ|tl|Panahong Meiji|tr|Meiji Dönemi|uk|Період Мейдзі|ur|میجی دور|vi|Thời kỳ Minh Trị|war|Panahon Meiji|wuu|明治|zh|明治|zh_classical|明治|zh_min_nan|Bêng-tī|zh_yue|明治|qid=Q3125096|lt=Meiji era}}, the Upper Shrine of Suwa's high priest or ''Ōhōri'' (大祝  'great priest'; also ''Ōhafuri'') was a young boy chosen from the [[Suwa clan]], who was, during his term of office, considered to be [[Arahitogami|a living god]], the visible incarnation or 'body' of the unseen god of the shrine.<ref name="Ihara">Ihara (2008). pp. 157–185.</ref><ref>{{cite book|date=1988|editor1-last=Hall|editor1-first=John Whitney|title=The Cambridge History of Japan, Volume 1: Ancient Japan|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0521223522|page=343|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=A3_6lp8IOK8C&pg=PA343}}</ref>

The legend of how Suwa Myōjin chose his first priest is recounted in various sources, such as the ''Suwa Daimyōjin Ekotoba'':

<blockquote>At the beginning of the god's [[Honji suijaku|manifestation]], he took off his robe, put them on an eight year old boy, and dubbed him 'great priest' (''Ōhōri''). The god declared, "I do not have a body and so make this priest (''hōri'') my body."<br />
This [boy] is Arikazu (有員), the priest of the sacred robe (御衣祝 ''Misogihōri''), the founding ancestor of the Miwa/Jin (神, i.e. Suwa) clan.{{efn|「祝は神明の垂迹の初。御衣を八歳の童男にぬぎきせ給ひて。大祝と称し。我において体なし。祝を以て躰とすと神勅ありけり。是則御衣祝有員神氏の始祖なり。」<ref name="EkotobaHori">''Suwa Daimyōjin Ekotoba'', in Hanawa (1919). pp. 521–522.</ref>}}</blockquote>

[[File:Suwa Daimyōjin - 諏訪大明神.jpg|thumb|200px|Suwa Myōjin as a warrior in hunting gear]]

35-36.</ref><ref>Miyasaka (1992), pp. 7–11.</ref>

One of these two texts is a genealogy of the Aso (阿蘇) clan of [[Aso Shrine]] in [[Kyushu]] known as the 異本阿蘇氏系図 (''Ihon Asoshi Keizu'').<ref>Kanai, Tenbi (2018). 諏訪信仰の性格とその変遷―諏訪信仰通史 (''Suwa shinkō no seikaku to sono hensen: Suwa shinko tsūshi''). in Kodai Buzoku Kenkyūkai, ed. pp. 36-38.</ref><ref name="Asoshi">''Ihon Asoshi Keizu'', cited in Kanai (1982). p. 109.</ref> It reads in part:

<blockquote>Otoei (''Ōhōri'' of the great god of Suwa): also known as Kumako (神子) or Kumako (熊古).<br />
When he was eight years old, the great god Minakatatomi-no-Mikoto appeared, took off his robe and put them on Kumako, declaring, "I do not have a body and so make you my body." In the third month of the second year of {{ill|Emperor Yōmei|ar|الإمبراطور يومي|arz|الامبراطور يومى|azb|یومی (ایمپیراتور)|bn|সম্রাট ইওমি|ckb|ئیمپراتۆر یۆمێی|cs|Jómei|de|Yōmei|es|Yōmei Tennō|fa|امپراتور یومی|fi|Yōmei|fr|Yōmei|id|Kaisar Yōmei|it|Yōmei|ja|用明天皇|ka|იომეი|ko|요메이 천황|nl|Yomei|pl|Yōmei|pt|Yomei|ru|Император Ёмэй|sh|Car Yōmei|simple|Emperor Yōmei|sl|Cesar Jomei|sv|Yomei|th|จักรพรรดิโยเม|tl|Emperador Yōmei|tr|Yōmei (imparator)|uk|Імператор Йомей|uz|Imperator Yōmei|vi|Thiên hoàng Yōmei|yo|Emperor Yōmei|zh|用明天皇|zh_min_nan|Yômei Thian-hông|zh_yue|用明天皇|qid=Q349281|lt=Iware Ikebe no Ōmiya}} (587), a sanctuary (社壇) was built at the foot of the mountain at the southern side of the lake (i.e. Lake Suwa) to worship the great god of Suwa and various other gods ...{{efn|「乙頴 (諏訪大神大祝)：一名神子、又云、熊古　生而八歳、御名方富命大神化現脱着御衣於神子勅曰、吾無体以汝為体、盤余池辺大宮朝二年丁未三月搆壇于湖南山麓、祭諏訪大明神及百八十神、奉千代田刺忌串斎之」<ref name="Asoshi" />}}</blockquote>

The other is the ''Ōhōri-ke Jinshi Keizu'' (大祝家神氏系図), a genealogy of the Suwa clan discovered in the ''Ōhōri''<nowiki />'s residence in 1884 ({{ill|Meiji era|ar|فترة مييجي|ast|Dómina Meiji|az|Meydzi dövrü|azb|مئی‌جی دؤورو|be|Перыяд Мэйдзі|bn|মেইজি যুগ|bo|མེའི་ཇིའི་དུས་དུས་མཚམས།|ca|Era Meiji|ceb|Panahon sa Meiji|cs|Období Meidži|da|Meiji-perioden|de|Meiji-Zeit|el|Μεϊτζί (περίοδος)|es|Era Meiji|et|Meiji periood|eu|Meiji Aroa|fa|دوره میجی|fi|Meiji-kausi|fr|Ère Meiji|gl|Período Meiji|he|תקופת מייג'י|hr|Meiji (razdoblje)|ht|Epòk Meiji|hu|Meidzsi-kor|id|Zaman Meiji|io|Ero Meiji|is|Meiji-tímabilið|it|Periodo Meiji|ja|明治|ka|მეიძის ეპოქა|kbp|Mejii wɛɛ yaa alɩwaatʊ|kk|Мэйдзи дәуірі|ko|메이지 시대|la|Aetas Meiji|lt|Meidži laikotarpis|lv|Meidzi periods|mk|Меиџи (период)|mn|Мэйжийн эрин|ms|Zaman Meiji|nl|Meijiperiode|nn|Meiji|no|Meiji-perioden|pl|Meiji (okres)|pt|Era Meiji|ro|Perioada Meiji|ru|Мэйдзи|simple|Meiji period|sk|Obdobie Meidži|sq|Periudha Meixhi|sr|Меиџи период|sv|Meijiperioden|ta|மெய்சி காலம்|th|ยุคเมจิ|tl|Panahong Meiji|tr|Meiji Dönemi|uk|Період Мейдзі|ur|میجی دور|vi|Thời kỳ Minh Trị|war|Panahon Meiji|wuu|明治|zh|明治|zh_classical|明治|zh_min_nan|Bêng-tī|zh_yue|明治|qid=Q3125096|lt=Meiji}} 17).<ref>Kanai, Tenbi (2018). In the second year of Emperor Yōmei, Kumako built a sanctuary at the foot of the mountain at the southern side of the lake.

====The King of Hadai====
A medieval Buddhist legend portrays Suwa Myōjin as a king from India who later achieved enlightenment and went to Japan [[Honji suijaku|to become a native ''kami'']].

A short text attached to a late 15th century copy of an ordinance regulating the Upper Shrine's ritual purity [[taboo]]s (物忌み ''monoimi'') originally enforced in 1238 and revised in 1317, the ''Suwa Kamisha monoimi no rei no koto'' (諏訪上社物忌令之事),<ref name="TakeiMasahiro">{{cite journal|last1=Takei|first1=Masahiro|title=祭事を読む-諏訪上社物忌令之事- (Saiji wo yomu: Suwa Kamisha monoimi no rei no koto)|journal=飯田市美術博物館 研究紀要 (Bulletin of the Iida City Museum)|date=1999|volume=9|pages=121–144|url=http://ci.nii.ac.jp/naid/110008434555}}</ref> relates that 'Takeminakata Myōjin' (武御名方明神) was originally the ruler of [[Mahajanapada|a certain Indian kingdom]] called 'Hadai' (波堤国 ''Hadai-koku''){{efn|This place name appears as one of the sixteen [[Mahajanapada|Mahājanapadas]] in {{ill|Kumārajīva|ar|كوماراجيفا|as|কুমাৰজীৱ|ast|Kumarajiva|bn|কুমারজীব|ca|Kumaradjiva|cs|Kumáradžíva|de|Kumārajīva|eo|Kumaraĝivo|es|Kumarajiva|eu|Kumarajiva|fa|کوماراجیوا|fr|Kumarajiva|gl|Kumārajīva|hi|कुमारजीव|hr|Kumārajīva|hu|Kumáradzsíva|id|Kumārajīva|it|Kumārajīva|ja|鳩摩羅什|kk|Кумаражива|kn|ಕುಮಾರಜೀವ|ko|쿠마라지바|mg|Kumarajiva|ml|കുമാരജീവൻ|nl|Kumarajiva|no|Kumārajīva|pa|ਕੁਮਾਰਜੀਵ|pl|Kumaradżiwa|ru|Кумараджива|sh|Kumārajīva|sl|Kumaradživa|sr|Kumarađiva|te|కుమారజీవుడు|th|พระกุมารชีพ|tr|Kumarajiva|uk|Кумараджива|ur|کماراجیوا|vi|Cưu-ma-la-thập|zh|鸠摩罗什|zh_classical|鳩摩羅什|zh_min_nan|Khiu-môo-lô-si̍p|zh_yue|鳩摩羅什|qid=Q335293|lt=Kumārajīva}}'s translation of the {{ill|Humane King Sutra|ja|仁王経|ko|인왕경|no|Prajñāpāramitāsūtraen om konger med medlidenhet|pt|Sutra do Rei Humano|zh|仁王护国经|qid=Q5939265|lt=Humane King Sutra}}.<ref>{{cite web|title=十六大国一覧表|url=http://www.sakya-muni.jp/pdf/mono15_s02_hu01.pdf|website=原始仏教聖典資料による釈尊伝の研究 (A Study of the Biography of Sakya-muni Based on the Early Buddhist Scriptural Sources)}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=佛說仁王般若波羅蜜經 第2卷|url=http://tripitaka.cbeta.org/T08n0245_002|website=CBETA (Chinese Buddhist Electronic Text Association) 漢文大藏經}}</ref>}} who survived an insurrection instigated by a rebel named 'Moriya' (守屋 or 守洩) during the king's absence while the latter was out hunting deer. After going to [[:en:Persia|Persia]] to rescue its inhabitants from an evil dragon, the king ruled over it for some time as 'Emperor Suwa' (陬波皇帝 ''Suwa Kōtei'') before retiring to "cultivate the seedling of virtue {{ill|Enlightenment in Buddhism|af|Verligting in Boeddhisme|ar|التنوير في البوذية|bcl|Kaliwanagan sa Budismo|bn|বোধোদয়|et|Virgumine|fa|روشنیدگی (بودیسم)|fr|Éveil (bouddhisme)|hu|Megvilágosodás a buddhizmusban|hy|Բուդդայական լուսավորություն|id|Pencerahan dalam Buddhisme|it|Illuminazione nel buddismo|ja|悟り|lt|Atbudimas (budizmas)|nl|Verlichting (boeddhisme)|no|Opplysning i buddhismen|ps|روښانتیا په بودیزم کې|ru|Просветление (буддизм)|simple|Enlightenment (Buddhism)|th|ตรัสรู้|uz|Buddizmda ma’rifat|vi|Giác ngộ trong Phật giáo|zh|开悟|qid=Q1137019|lt=and realize the Buddhist path}}." He eventually manifested in Japan, appearing in various places before finally choosing to dwell in Suwa.<ref name="chusei">Fukuda; Nihonmatsu; Tokuda, eds. (2015). pp. 114-116.</ref><ref name="Takei129130">Takei (1999), pp. 129–130.</ref><ref name="Miyachi84">Miyaji (1931b).  p. 84.</ref>

At that time, a traitorous vassal named Bikyō (美教) suddenly organized an army and sought to kill the king. Brahmā then saw this and commanded the [[Four Heavenly Kings|four great deva-kings]] to wield {{ill|Vajra|ar|فاجرا|bn|বজ্র|bo|རྡོ་རྗེ།|ca|Vajra|cs|Vadžra|de|Vajra|eo|Kloŝo kaj vajra|es|Vajra|et|Vadžra|eu|Vajra|fi|Vajra|fr|Vajra|hi|वज्र|hu|Vadzsra|id|Wajra|it|Vajra|ja|金剛杵|jv|Wajra|ka|ვაჯრა|kk|Ваджра|km|វិជ្រៈ|kn|ವಜ್ರಾಯುಧ|ko|바즈라|lt|Vadžra|mdf|Ваджра|mr|वज्र|ms|Vajra|ne|बज्र|nl|Vajra|no|Vajra|pa|ਵਜਰ|pl|Dordże|pt|Vajra|ro|Vajra|ru|Ваджра|si|වජ්‍රායුධය ( වජ්‍රය )|sv|Vajra|ta|வஜ்ராயுதம்|te|వజ్రాయుధం|th|วัชระ|tr|Vajra|tt|Ваджра|uk|Ваджра|vi|Kim cương chử|wuu|金刚|zh|金剛|zh_yue|金剛 (佛教)|qid=Q695709|lt=Vajra}}-poles and destroy the army. Regarding the Upper Shrine's hunting rituals, the ''Monoimi no rei'' asserts that

<blockquote>[The shrine's] hunts began in the deer park of Hadai-no-kuni [in India]. [The use of] hawks began in [[Magadha|Magada-no-kuni]].<ref>Grumbach (2005). p. 206.</ref></blockquote>

[[File:Shaka Nyorai.jpg|thumb|120px|Medieval Buddhist legends claim the Suwa deity to be a relative of [[:en:Gautama Buddha|Gautama Buddha]] (pictured)]]
The second half of the legend (the slaying of the dragon in Persia and the king's migration to Japan) is used by the ''Ekotoba''<nowiki />'s compiler, Suwa Enchū, in a liturgical text, the ''Suwa Daimyōjin Kōshiki'' (諏方大明神講式),<ref name="Koshikitaikei">諏方大明神講式 (''Suwa Daimyōjin Kōshiki''), in {{cite book|editor1-last=Takeuchi|editor1-first=Hideo|title=神道大系 神社編30 諏訪 (Shintō Taikei, Jinja-hen vol. 30: Suwa)|date=1982|publisher=Shintō Taikei Hensankai}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=諏方大明神講式 (''Suwa Daimyōjin Kōshiki'')|url=http://base1.nijl.ac.jp/iview/Frame.jsp?DB_ID=G0003917KTM&C_CODE=KSRM-287105&IMG_SIZE=&PROC_TYPE=null&SHOMEI=%E3%80%90%E8%AB%8F%E6%96%B9%E5%A4%A7%E6%98%8E%EF%A8%99%E8%AC%9B%E5%BC%8F%E3%80%91&REQUEST_MARK=null&OWNER=null&IMG_NO=4|website=国文学研究資料館 (National Institute of Japanese Literature)}}</ref><ref name="chusei" /> where it is introduced as an alternative, if somewhat less credible, account of the Suwa deity's origins (in comparison to the myth of Takeminakata of Izumo as found in the ''Kuji Hongi'', touted by the same text as the authoritative origin story of the god) that nevertheless should not be suppressed.<ref>Fukuda; Nihonmatsu; Tokuda, eds. (2015). p. 116.</ref> In this text, the king of Hadai is claimed to be a great-great-grandson of {{ill|Sihahanu|eo|Sinhahanuo|ko|시하하누|my|သီဟဟနု|ru|Шихаханью|th|พระเจ้าสีหหนุ|vi|Sihahanu|qid=Q7513387|lt=King Siṃhahanu}} (獅子頬王 ''Shishikyō-ō''), [[:en:Gautama Buddha|Gautama Buddha]]'s grandfather.<ref>Fukuda; Nihonmatsu; Tokuda, eds. (2015). p. 115.</ref> Bikyō, the rebel who raised up an army against the king in India - identified as an incarnation of the {{ill|Mara (demon)|af|Mara (demoon)|bn|মার|cs|Mára|da|Mara (buddhisme)|de|Mara (Buddhismus)|eo|Marao|es|Mara (budismo)|et|Māra (budism)|fa|ماره|fi|Mara (demoni)|fr|Māra|he|מארה (בודהיזם)|hi|मार (राक्षस)|hu|Mára (démon)|hy|Մարա (դև)|id|Māra|it|Māra|ja|マーラ|kk|Мара|ko|마라 파피야스|la|Mara (daemon)|lt|Mara (budizmas)|mk|Мара (демон)|mr|मार (राक्षस)|my|မာရ်နတ်|nl|Mara (deva)|no|Mara (demon)|pl|Mara (religie Wschodu)|pt|Mara (budismo)|ro|Mara (budism)|ru|Мара (буддизм)|sh|Mara (demon)|sr|Мара (будизам)|sv|Mara (buddhism)|ta|மாறன், பௌத்தம்|th|มาร (ศาสนาพุทธ)|tl|Mara (demonyo)|uk|Мара (буддизм)|ur|مار (شیطان)|vi|Thiên ma Ba Tuần|zh|天魔|zh_yue|天魔|qid=Q1352021|lt=Demon King}} (魔王) - is also said to have eventually manifested in Japan, opposing the deity in Suwa as "Moriya the evil outlaw."<ref>Fukuda; Nihonmatsu; Tokuda, eds. (2015). pp. 114-115.</ref>

A similar account appears in a work known as the ''Suwa Jinja Engi'' (諏訪神社縁起) or ''Suwa Shintō Engi'' (諏訪神道縁起),<ref>''Suwa Jinja Engi'' (諏訪神社縁起 上下卷), in {{cite book |editor1-last=Suwa Kyōikukai |title=諏訪史料叢書 巻26 (Suwa Shiryō Soshō, vol. 26) |date=1937 |publisher=Suwa Kōikukai |pages=54–64 |url=http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/1185900/41}}</ref> wherein the Suwa deity is identified as the son of Kibonnō (貴飯王), the son of Amṛtodana (甘呂飯王 ''Kanrobonnō''), one of Siṃhahanu's four sons. The Lower Shrine's goddess, meanwhile, is the daughter of {{ill|Pasenadi|as|পসেনদি|be|Пасенадзі|bn|পসেনদি|bo|ཀོ་ས་ལའི་རྒྱལ་པོ་རབ་གསལ་|eo|Prasenaĝito|es|Pasenadi|fr|Pasenadi|hi|प्रसेनजित्|id|Pasenadi|ja|プラセーナジット|km|បសេនទិកោសល|kn|ಪಸೇನದಿ|ko|파세나디|my|ပသေနဒိကောသလမင်း|ru|Пасенади|ta|பசேனதி|th|พระเจ้าปเสนทิโกศล|ur|پاسیناڈی|vi|Ba-tư-nặc|zh|波斯匿王|qid=Q3055324|lt=Prasenajit}} (波斯匿王 ''Hashinoku-ō''), claimed here to be the son of Dronodana (黒飯王 ''Kokubonnō''), another son of Siṃhananu.<ref>Miyaji (1931b). p. 85.</ref>

=====The ''Suwa Mishirushibumi''=====

During the Misayama festival as performed during the medieval period, the ''Ōhōri'' recited a [[Norito|ritual declaration]] supposedly composed by the Suwa deity himself known as the ''Suwa Mishirushibumi'' (陬波御記文),<ref>Text and commentary in Kanai (1982). pp. 162-172.</ref> which begins:

<blockquote>I, Great King Suwa (陬波大王), have hidden my person during [[Sexagenary cycle|[the year/month/day of] the Yang Wood Horse]] (甲午 ''kinoe-uma'').<br />
[The name] 'Suwa' (陬波) and [the sign] Yang Wood Horse [and] the seal (印文){{efn|The 'seal' referred to here is interpreted to be either the Upper Shrine's sacred seal made of deer antler<ref>Kanai (1982). p. 167.</ref> or the ''Mishirushibumi'' itself.<ref>Fukuda; Nihonmatsu; Tokuda, eds. (2015). pp. 117-118.</ref>}} - these three are all one and the same.{{efn|「陬波大王　限甲午隠身、陬波与甲午　印文同一物三名。」<ref>Kanai (1982). p. 163.</ref>}}</blockquote>
[[File:Yabusame00.jpg|thumb|left|[[Yabusame]] archers in hunting gear, Edo period]]
Within the text, King Suwa (i.e. Suwa Myōjin) declares the ''Ōhōri'' to be his 'true [[Shintai|body]]' (真神体 ''shin no shintai'') and the Misayama (三斎山) hunting grounds below Yatsugatake (here likened to {{ill|Vulture Peak|bn|গৃধ্রশৃঙ্গ|ca|Pic dels voltors|eo|Gipopinto|et|Pistriku mäetipp|fr|Pic des Vautours|hi|गृद्धकूट पर्वत|id|Puncak Burung Nasar|it|Gṛdhrakūṭaparvata|ja|霊鷲山|ko|영취산 (인도)|my|ဂိဇ္ဈကုဋ်တောင်|no|Gribbenes fjelltopp|si|ගිජ්ඣකූටය|ta|கழுகு சிகரம்|th|เขาคิชฌกูฏ (ภูเขาในศาสนาพุทธ)|uk|Пік Грифа|vi|Gijjhakūṭa|zh|灵鹫山 (印度)|qid=Q19755572|lt=Vulture Peak}} in India) to be another manifestation of himself that cleanses (斎) the three (三) evils: {{ill|Manasa, vacha, karmana|bn|মনস, বাচ, কর্মণ|hi|मनस, वाचा, कार्मण|tt|Манаса, вача, кармана|uk|Manasa, vāchā, kārmana|qid=Q16920548|lt=evil thoughts, evil speech and evil actions}}.<ref>Fukuda; Nihonmatsu; Tokuda, eds. (2015). pp. 119-120.</ref><ref>Kanai (1982). pp. 168-169.</ref> He promises that whoever sets foot at Misayama will not fall into [[Saṃsāra (Buddhism)#Realms of rebirth|the lower, evil realms of existence]] (悪趣 ''akushu''); conversely, the god condemns and disowns whoever defiles the hunting grounds by cutting down its trees or digging out the soil.<ref name="Kanai169">Kanai (1982). p. 169.</ref>

A commentary on the ''Mishirushibumi'', the ''Suwa Shichū'' (陬波私注 "Personal Notes on the ''Suwa Mishirusibumi''," written 1313–1314),<ref name="KanaiShichu">Text and commentary in Kanai (1982). pp. 173-187.</ref> elaborates on the text by retelling the legend of Suwa Myōjin's consecration of his first priest:

<blockquote>The ''Daimyōjin'' was born during [the year/month/day of] the Yang Wood Horse and disappeared during [the year/month/day of] the Yang Wood Horse.<br />
Sokutan Daijin (続旦大臣) was the Daimyōjin's uncle who accompanied him from India. When the Daimyōjin was to disappear, he took off his garments, put them on the Daijin, and dubbed him the ''Misogihōri'' (御衣木法理). He then pronounced a vow: "You shall consider this priest to be my body."{{efn|「一、大明神甲午<sub>仁</sub>有御誕生甲午<sub>仁</sub>隠御身給<sub>フ</sub><br />
一、続旦（ソクタン）大臣<small>ト</small>申<small>ハ</small>大明神<small>ノ</small>叔父御前自<sub>リ</sub>天竺御同道、大明神御体<sub>ヲ</sub>隠<sub>サセ</sub>給<sub>シ</sub>時御装束ヲ奉抜著（ヌキキセ）彼大臣給<small>テ</small>号御衣木（ミソキ）法理<small>ト</small> 我之躰以法理<small>ヲ</small>躰<small>ト</small>セヨトハ誓給<sub>シ</sub>也」<ref>Kanai (1982). pp. 173-174.</ref>}}</blockquote>

The same text identifies the god's uncle Sokutan Daijin with Arikazu.<ref>Fukuda; Nihonmatsu; Tokuda, eds. (2015). pp. 117, 119.</ref><ref>Kanai (1982). pp. 176-177.</ref>{{efn|「一、御衣木法理殿御実名<sub>ハ</sub>者有員<sub>云〻</sub>」<ref>Kanai (1982). p. 175.</ref>}}

Buddhist concept of the {{ill|Three poisons|bn|ত্রিবিষ|de|Drei Geistesgifte|es|Tres venenos|et|Kolm meelemürki|fa|سه زهر|fr|Trois poisons|he|שלושת הרעלים (בודהיזם)|hi|त्रिविष|hu|Három méreg|id|Tiga ====The dragon (serpent) deity of Suwa====
[[File:Suwa taisha Kamisha Honmiya , 諏訪大社 上社 本宮 - panoramio (30).jpg|thumb|left|''{{ill|Chōzuya|bcl|Chōzuya|es|Chōzuya|fa|تمیزویا|fr|Chōzuya|id|Chōzuya|it|Chōzuya|ja|手水|ko|데미즈야|oc|Chōzuya|ro|Chōzuya|ru|Тэмидзуя|simple|Chōzuya|zh|手水舍|qid=Q1069667|lt=Chōzuya}}'' with a dragon-shaped spout, ''Kamisha Honmiya'']]
Folk belief has long held the god of Suwa Shrine to assume the form of a serpent or dragon. Consequently, the deity appears as such in a number of folktales and anecdotes.

In one such story, Suwa Myōjin once came to {{ill|Izumo Province|ar|إزومو (مقاطعة)|ca|Província d'Izumo|cs|Provincie Izumo|de|Provinz Izumo|es|Provincia de Izumo|fa|ولایت ایزومو|fr|Province d'Izumo|gl|Provincia de Izumo|id|Provinsi Izumo|it|Izumo (provincia)|ja|出雲国|ka|იზუმოს პროვინცია|ko|이즈모국|lt|Idzumo žemė|nl|Izumo (provincie)|no|Izumo|pt|Província de Izumo|ru|Идзумо (провинция)|simple|Izumo Province|sk|Izumo (provincia)|sr|Провинција Изумо|tr|Izumo (vilayet)|uk|Провінція Ідзумо|wuu|出云国|zh|出雲國|zh_classical|出雲國|zh_min_nan|Izumo-kok|zh_yue|出雲國|qid=Q582846|lt=Izumo Province}} in the form of a dragon so gigantic that only his head can be seen; his tail was still at Suwa, caught in a tall pine tree by the shores of the lake. The other gods, upon seeing him, were so astounded and frightened at his enormous size that they exempted him from attending their yearly meetings.<ref>Matsutani, Miyoko (1960). ''Shinano no minwa'' (信濃の民話). Miraisha. p. 48, cited in Kanai (1982). p. 7.</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Shinano no kuni no Kannazuki (信濃の国の神無月)|url=http://minwa.fujipan.co.jp/area/nagano_012/|website=Fuji Baking Co., Ltd.|access-date=January 5, 2017|archive-date=January 5, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170105180141/http://minwa.fujipan.co.jp/area/nagano_012/|url-status=dead}}</ref> Thus, the deity of Suwa is claimed to be one of the very few ''kami'' in Japan who do not leave their shrines during the month of [[Kannazuki]], when most gods are thought to gather at Izumo and thus are absent from most of the country. The supposed tree where the dragon's tail was caught (currently reduced to a stump) is locally known as {{nihongo|''Okakematsu''|尾掛松}}.<ref>{{cite web|title=Okakematsu (尾掛松)|url=http://suwaarea-examine.com/okakematu.html|website=Mahoroba Suwa-ken (まほろば諏訪圏)|access-date=2015-01-05}}</ref>

A variant of this story transposes the setting from Izumo to the [[Kyoto Imperial Palace|Imperial Palace]] in Another popular story promulgated by wandering preachers associated with the shrines of Suwa during the medieval period claimed the Suwa deity to have originally been [[Kōga Saburō]], a warrior who temporarily became a dragon or a snake after a journey into the underworld.<ref>Miyasaka (1987). pp. 51-54.</ref><ref name="BreenTeeuwen2000">{{cite book|author1=John Breen|author2=Mark Teeuwen|title=Shinto in History: Ways of the Kami|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=MADlfH002mAC&pg=PA35|date=January 2000|publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=978-0-8248-2363-4|page=35}}</ref><ref name="Blacker2004">{{cite book|author=Carmen Blacker|title=The Catalpa Bow: A Study of Shamanistic Practices in Japan|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=mR6PAgAAQBAJ&pg=RA1-PA134|date=2 August 2004|publisher=Routledge|isbn=1-135-31872-7}}</ref><ref>Kanai (1982). pp. 278–317.</ref>

====''Omiwatari''====
[[File:180205 Lake Suwa omiwatari 03.jpg|thumb|''Omiwatari'']]
{{ill|Pressure ridge (ice)|az|Toros|be|Тарос|bg|Тороси|de|Presseishügel|fr|Ride de pression (glace)|ja|プレッシャー・リッジ|ka|ტოროსი|kk|Торос|lv|Toross|nn|Skruis|no|Skrugard|pl|Toros (glacjologia)|ru|Торосы|sah|Торуос|uk|Тороси|qid=Q3134007|lt=Cracks and ridges}} that form on a frozen {{ill|Lake Suwa|ar|بحيرة سوا|arz|بحيره سوا|ceb|Suwa Ko|de|Suwa-See|eo|Suŭa-Lago|es|Lago Suwa|et|Suwa järv|eu|Suwa aintzira|fa|دریاچه سووا|fr|Lac Suwa|id|Danau Suwa|ja|諏訪湖|ko|스와호|lt|Suva (ežeras)|mk|Сува (езеро)|my|ဆုဝကန်|nn|Suwasjøen|pl|Suwa (jezioro)|ro|Lacul Suwa|ru|Сува (озеро)|sr|Језеро Сува|th|ทะเลสาบซูวะ|tr|Suwa Gölü|vi|Hồ Suwa|zh|諏訪湖|zh_yue|諏訪湖|qid=Q1206692|lt=Lake Suwa}} during cold winters have traditionally been interpreted as the trail left behind by Suwa Myōjin as he leaves the ''Upper Shrine'' and crosses the lake to meet his wife enshrined on the Lower Shrine on the opposite (northern) shore.<ref name="railways1922">{{cite book|author=Japan. Dept. of railways|title=The Hot Springs of Japan (and the Principal Cold Springs) Including Chosen (Korea) Taiwan (Formosa) South Manchuria, Together with Many Tables Giving Classification, Chemical Basis, Curative Values, Radio-activity, Etc. 196 Illustrations, 15 Maps, Specially Drawn, 2 Colored Lithographs|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=smA0AAAAMAAJ|year=1922|page=194}}</ref> Called ''Omiwatari'' (御神渡 'the god's crossing' or 'the god's pathway'), the cracks were considered to be a good omen for the coming year.<ref name="JapanTimes">{{cite news|title=Ice phenomenon warms up hearts in the Lake Suwa region|url=http://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2012/03/03/national/ice-phenomenon-warms-up-hearts-in-the-lake-suwa-region/#.WRpvc9SLRRA|agency=The Japan Times|date=2012-03-03}}</ref> The priests of the Grand Shrine of Suwa traditionally used the crack's appearance to divine the quality of the year's harvest.<ref name="Miyasaka3840">Miyasaka (1992). pp. 38-40.</ref> For the locals, the crack also served as a sign that the frozen lake was safe to walk upon.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Brazil|first1=Mark|title=Omi-watari|url=http://www.japanvisitor.com/about-japan/omi-watari|website=Japan Visitor}}</ref><ref>Miyasaka (1992). p. 42.</ref> Conversely, the ''omiwatari''<nowiki/>'s failure to appear at all (明海 ''ake no umi'') or the cracks forming in an unusual way were held to be a sign of bad luck for the year.<ref name="Miyasaka3840" />

Since the late 20th century, the ''omiwatari'' has become a much rarer sight than it was in the past due to rising temperatures caused by {{ill|Global warming|af|Aardverwarming|als|Globale ====As god of war====
[[File:Sakanoue Tamuramaro sw.jpg|thumb|150px|left|[[Sakanoue no Tamuramaro]] is credited with instituting the religious festivities of Suwa Shrine after the god of Suwa came to his aid against the {{ill|Emishi|ar|إيميشي|ca|Emishi|cs|Emiši|de|Ezo (Volk)|es|Emishi|eu|Emishi|fa|امیشی|fr|Emishi|gl|Emishi|id|Emishi|it|Emishi|ja|蝦夷|ko|에조|nl|Emishi|no|Emishi|pl|Emishi|pt|Emishi|ru|Эмиси|sr|Емиши|tr|Emishi|uk|Емісі|wuu|虾夷|zh|蝦夷|zh_min_nan|Emisi|zh_yue|蝦夷|qid=Q932574|lt=Emishi}} peoples.]]
Suwa Myōjin is also considered to be a {{ill|List of war deities|ar|قائمة آلهة الحرب|arz|الهة الحرب|et|Sõjajumal|pt|Deidade bélica|tr|Savaş tanrıları listesi|qid=Q1752560|lt=god of war}}, one of a number of such deities in the Japanese pantheon.
