The ''[[Taiheiki]]'' recounts a story where a five-colored cloud resembling a serpent (a manifestation of the god) rose up from {{ill|Lake Suwa|ar|بحيرة سوا|arz|بحيره سوا|ceb|Suwa Ko|de|Suwa-See|eo|Suŭa-Lago|es|Lago Suwa|et|Suwa järv|eu|Suwa aintzira|fa|دریاچه سووا|fr|Lac Suwa|id|Danau Suwa|ja|諏訪湖|ko|스와호|lt|Suva (ežeras)|mk|Сува (езеро)|my|ဆုဝကန်|nn|Suwasjøen|pl|Suwa (jezioro)|ro|Lacul Suwa|ru|Сува (озеро)|sr|Језеро Сува|th|ทะเลสาบซูวะ|tr|Suwa Gölü|vi|Hồ Suwa|zh|諏訪湖|zh_yue|諏訪湖|qid=Q1206692|lt=Lake Suwa}} and spread away westward to assist the Japanese army against the Mongols.<ref>De Visser (1913). p. 202.</ref><ref>Ōbayashi (1987). p. 96.</ref>

<blockquote>On the seventh day, when the Imperial devotions were completed, from Lake Suwa there arose a cloud of many colours, in shape like a great serpent, which spread away towards the west. The doors of the Temple-treasury of [[Hachiman]] flew open, and the skies were filled with a sound of galloping horses and of ringing bits. In {{ill|Hiyoshi Taisha|az|Hiyoşi məbədi|de|Hiyoshi-Taisha|fa|هیوشی تایشا|fr|Hiyoshi-taisha|hu|Hie-nagyszentély|ja|日吉大社|ka|ჰიიოში ტაიშა|ko|히요시타이샤|ru|Хиёси-тайся|tr|Hiyoshi Taisha|zh|日吉大社|qid=Q656451|lt=the twenty-one shrines of Yoshino}} the brocade-curtained mirrors moved, the swords of the Temple-treasury put on a sharp edge, and all the shoes offered to the god turned towards the west. At [[:en:Sumiyoshi taisha|Sumiyoshi]] sweat poured from below the saddles of the four horses sacred to the deities, and the iron shields turned of themselves and faced the enemy in a line.<ref>{{cite web|title=太平記 巻第三十九|url=http://j-texts.com/taihei/tk39.html|website=J-TEXTS 日本文学電子図書館|date=December 30, 2020 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Aston|first1=William George|title=A History of Japanese Literature|date=2015|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-1108081061|page=181|edition=reprint|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xxxoBgAAQBAJ&pg=PA181}}</ref></blockquote>

==Analysis==
===Takeminakata in the ''Kojiki''===
[[Image:Ono-Yasumaro.jpg|thumb|right|{{ill|Ō no Yasumaro|be|О-но Ясумара|ca|Ō no Yasumaro|ckb|ئۆ نۆ یاسومارۆ|de|Ō no Yasumaro|eo|O no Jasumaro|es|Ō no Yasumaro|fa|اونو یاسومارو|fr|Ō no Yasumaro|gl|Ō-No-Yasumaro|it|Ō no Yasumaro|ja|太安万侶|ko|오노 야스마로|oc|O no Yasumaro|pl|Ō-no Yasumaro|pt|Ō no Yasumaro|ru|О-но Ясумаро|uk|О но Ясумаро|zh|太安萬侶|qid=Q384705|lt=Ō no Yasumaro}}, the compiler of the ''Kojiki'']]

Takeminakata's abrupt appearance in the ''Kojiki''<nowiki />'s version of the ''kuni-yuzuri'' myth has long puzzled scholars, as the god is mentioned nowhere else in the work, including the genealogy of Ōkuninushi's progeny that precedes the ''kuni-yuzuri'' narrative proper.<ref>Chamberlain (1882). [http://sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj033.htm Section XXVI.—The Deities the August Descendants of the Deity Master-of-the-Great-Land.]</ref> Aside from the parallel account contained in the ''Kuji Hongi'' (which was itself based on the ''Kojiki''<ref name="Suwashishi2">Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai, ed. (1995). pp. 684-685, 687.</ref>), he is altogether absent from the ''Nihon Shoki''<nowiki />'s version of the myth.<ref>{{cite wikisource |Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |chapter=Book II |author=Aston, William George |date=1896 |pages=68–70}}</ref><ref>Miyasaka (1987). p. 18.</ref> Early documents from Izumo such as the province's ''[[Fudoki]]'' also fail to mention any god named '(Take)minakata', nor is there apparently any sign of Takeminakata worship in Izumo in antiquity.<ref name="Suwashishi2" />

Pre-modern authors such as {{ill|Motoori Norinaga|ar|موتوري نوريناغا|bg|Мотоори Норинага|de|Motoori Norinaga|es|Motoori Norinaga|fa|موتوئوری نوریناگا|fi|Motoori Norinaga|fr|Motoori Norinaga|gl|Motoori Norinaga|hu|Motoori Norinaga|it|Motoori Norinaga|ja|本居宣長|ka|მოტოორი ნორინაგა|ko|모토오리 노리나가|lt|Norinaga Motoori|mt|Motoori Norinaga|pl|Norinaga Motoori|pt|Motoori Norinaga|ro|Motoori Norinaga|ru|Мотоори Норинага|simple|Motoori Norinaga|sl|Motoori Norinaga|th|โมโตริ โนรินางะ|tr|Motoori Norinaga|uk|Мотоорі Норінаґа|zh|本居宣長|qid=Q384647|lt=Motoori Norinaga}} tended to explain Takeminakata's absence outside of the ''Kojiki'' and the ''Kuji Hongi'' by conflating the god with certain obscure deities found in other sources thought to share certain similar characteristics (e.g. [[Isetsuhiko]]).<ref name="Norinaga3">Motoori, Norinaga (1937). [http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/1109355/81 古事記傳 (''Kojiki-den''), vol. 14] in Motoori Toyokai (ed.), 本居宣長全集 (''Motoori Norinaga Zenshū''), vol. 2. Tokyo: Yoshikawa Kōbunkan. pp. 683–684. (Original work written 1764–1798)</ref> While a few modern scholars still suppose some kind of indirect connection between the deity and Izumo by postulating that Takeminakata's origins lie either in peoples that migrated from Izumo northwards to Suwa and the {{ill|Hokuriku region|ar|منطقة هوكوريكو|bar|Hokuriku|bg|Хокурику|ca|Hokuriku|ckb|ناوچەی ھۆکوریکو|cs|Hokuriku|de|Hokuriku|eo|Hokuriku|es|Región de Hokuriku|eu|Hokuriku eskualdea|fa|منطقه هوکوریکو|fi|Hokuriku|fr|Région du Hokuriku|hr|Hokuriku (regija)|id|Wilayah Hokuriku|ilo|Rehion ti Hokuriku|it|Hokuriku|ja|北陸地方|ko|호쿠리쿠 지방|lt|Hokuriku regionas|mk|Хокурику|nl|Hokuriku|pl|Region Hokuriku|pt|Hokuriku (região)|ru|Хокурику (регион)|sh|Hokuriku|sk|Hokuriku|sv|Hokuriku|th|โฮกูริกุ|tl|Hokuriku|tr|Hokuriku|ur|ہوکوریکو علاقہ|zh|北陸地方|qid=Q381025|lt=Hokuriku region}}<ref>Muraoka (1969). pp. 60-66.</ref> or in Hokuriku itself (the ancient {{ill|Koshi Province (Japan)|de|Provinz Koshi (Japan)|es|Provincia de Koshi (Japón)|ff|Koshi Province (Japan)|fr|Province de Koshi (Japon)|ja|越国|ko|고시국|nl|Koshi (provincie)|pt|Província de Koshi|simple|Koshi Province (Japan)|zh|越國 (日本)|zh_min_nan|Kosi-kok|zh_yue|越國 (日本)|qid=Q1351611|lt=province of Koshi}}, a region apparently once under Izumo's {{ill|Sphere of influence|ar|منطقة نفوذ|az|Təsir dairəsi|be|Сфера ўплыву|bg|Сфера на влияние|br|Kelc'h levezon|ca|Esfera d'influència|ckb|گۆڕەپانی دەسڕۆیی|cs|Sféra vlivu|cy|Cylch dylanwad|de|Interessensphäre|el|Σφαίρα επιρροής|eo|Influsfero|es|Esfera de influencia|eu|Eragin eremu|fa|منطقه نفوذ|fi|Etupiiri|fr|Sphère d'influence|gl|Esfera de influencia|he|אזור השפעה|hi|प्रभावक्षेत्र|hy|Ազդեցության ոլորտ|id|Lingkup pengaruh|it|Sfera di influenza|ja|勢力圏|kk|Ықпал аясы|ko|영향권|lv|Ietekmes zona|mk|Сфера на влијание|ms|Lingkungan pengaruh|nl|Invloedssfeer|no|Interessesfære|pnb|حلقہ اثر|ps|د نفوذ سيمه|pt|Esfera de სფერო|zh|勢力範圍|zh_yue|勢力範圍|qid=Q593682|lt=Sphere of influence}} as can be inferred from the myth of Ōkuninushi's marriage to Nunakawahime),<ref>Kanai (1982). pp. 8-9.</ref> others instead propose that the connection between Takeminakata and Izumo is an artificial construct by the ''Kojiki''<nowiki/>'s compilers.<ref name="Suwashishi2" /><ref name="Yoshii" /><ref name="Matsumae">{{cite book|author=Matsumae, Takeshi|title=Nihon shinwa no nazo ga yoku wakaru hon (日本神話の謎がよく分かる本)|date=2007|publisher=Daiwa Shobō (大和書房)|isbn=978-4-479-39166-1|pages=136–137}}</ref><ref name="miyachi90101">Miyaji (1931). pp. 90-101.</ref>

The contest between Takeminakata and Takemikazuchi - an element absent in other versions of the ''kuni-yuzuri'' myth cycle - is often explained as being either a new myth invented to serve the interests of the imperial court and the [[Fujiwara clan]], descendants of the [[Nakatomi clan]] that had worshiped Takemikazuchi as a [[Ujigami|patron deity]]<ref name="miyachi90101"/> (indeed, in other versions it is the god [[Futsunushi]] that takes center stage rather than Takemikazuchi, who is believed to have taken on Futsunushi's roles and attributes after the Nakatomi rose to power<ref>{{cite web |last1=Kadoya |first1=Atsushi |title=Futsunushi |url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=54 |website=Encyclopedia of Shinto |publisher=Kokugakuin University |access-date=2019-07-08}}</ref>), or an adaptation/reversal of a myth concerning a battle between an interloping god and a local deity preserved in the Suwa region (see below), with Takeminakata (the invading conqueror in Suwa myth) being recast into the role of the subjugated earthly ''kami''.<ref>Miyasaka (1987). pp. 30-33.</ref>

=== Suwa Myōjin and Moriya ===
[[File:Yasaka-no-Suzu - 八栄の鈴.jpg|thumb|The ''yasaka no suzu'' (八栄の鈴), a set of bronze [[Suzu (bell)|bells]] reputed in legend to have been brought to Suwa by Suwa Myōjin. In actuality, the bells date from the early {{ill|Heian period|ar|فترة هييآن|ast|Periodu Heian|az|Heyan dövrü|bcl|Panahon ni Heian|bg|Хеян|bn|হেইআন যুগ|br|Marevezh Heian|ca|Període Heian|ceb|Panahon sa Heian|cs|Období Heian|de|Heian-Zeit|el|Περίοδος Χεϊάν|eo|Epoko Heian|es|Período Heian|eu|Heian aroa|fa|دوره هی‌آن|fi|Heian-kausi|fr|Époque de Heian|gl|Período Heian|he|תקופת הייאן|hi|हेआन काल|hr|Heian (razdoblje)|hu|Heian-kor|hy|Հեիան ժամանակաշրջան|id|Zaman Heian|it|Periodo Heian|ja|平安時代|ka|ჰეიანის პერიოდი|ko|헤이안 시대|la|Aevum Heian|lt|Hejano laikotarpis|mn|Хэйан|mr|हियन कालावधी|ms|Zaman Heian|my|ဟဲအိအန်ခေတ်|nl|Heianperiode|nn|Heian|no|Heian-perioden|oc|Epòca d'Heian|pl|Heian|ps|هېيان دوره|pt|Período Heian|ro|Perioada Heian|ru|Период Хэйан|sh|Heianski period|simple|Heian period|sk|Obdobie Heian|sl|Obdobje Heian|sq|Periudha Heian|sr|Хеиан период|sv|Heian|ta|ஹையன் காலகட்டம்|th|ยุคเฮอัง|tl|Panahong Heian|tr|Heian Dönemi|uk|Період Хейан|vi|Thời kỳ Heian|war|Panahon Heian|wuu|平安时代|zh|平安时代|zh_classical|平安朝|zh_min_nan|Heian sî-tāi|zh_yue|平安時代|qid=Q193292|lt=Heian period}}.]]
The myth of Takeminakata's (Suwa Myōjin's) arrival in Suwa and his defeat of the god Moriya has been interpreted as the mythicization of a historical event in which a local lineage of chieftains who ruled the Suwa area was subjugated by invading outsiders, who subsequently set themselves up as the new rulers of the region - all the while still retaining the subjugated clan in an important position as the wielder of spiritual and ritual authority. This theory explains the relation between the Suwa (Miwa/Jin) and Moriya priestly families of the Upper Shrine of Suwa as that of the Moriya clan being the regional power supplanted by the newly arrived Miwa (Suwa) clan.

[[File:Ina Valley Relief Map, SRTM.jpg|thumb|left|190px|Relief map of the Ina Valley. {{ill|Lake Suwa|ar|بحيرة سوا|arz|بحيره سوا|ceb|Suwa Ko|de|Suwa-See|eo|Suŭa-Lago|es|Lago Suwa|et|Suwa järv|eu|Suwa aintzira|fa|دریاچه سووا|fr|Lac Suwa|id|Danau Suwa|ja|諏訪湖|ko|스와호|lt|Suva (ežeras)|mk|Сува (езеро)|my|ဆုဝကန်|nn|Suwasjøen|pl|Suwa (jezioro)|ro|Lacul Suwa|ru|Сува (озеро)|sr|Језеро Сува|th|ทะเลสาบซูวะ|tr|Suwa Gölü|vi|Hồ Suwa|zh|諏訪湖|zh_yue|諏訪湖|qid=Q1206692|lt=Lake Suwa}} can be seen at top right.]]
While one theory places this event during the end of the [[Jōmon period]], thus portraying the new arrivals as {{ill|Agrarian society|ar|مجتمع زراعي|az|Aqrar cəmiyyət|be|Аграрнае грамадства|bn|কৃষিভিত্তিক সমাজ|ckb|کۆمەڵگای کشتوکاڵی|cs|Agrární společnost|da|Landbrugssamfund|de|Agrargesellschaft|eo|Agrikultura socio|es|Sociedad agraria|et|Agraarühiskond|fa|جامعه زراعی|fi|Maatalousyhteiskunta|fr|Société agraire|hi|कृषिक समाज|hy|Ագրարային հասարակություն|id|Masyarakat agraris|ja|農耕社会|kk|Аграрлы қоғам|ko|농경 사회|lv|Agrāra sabiedrība|ms|Kerajaan agraria|nl|Agrarische samenleving|pl|Społeczeństwo rolnicze|pt|Sociedade agrária|ru|Аграрное общество|sv|Jordbrukssamhälle|th|สังคมเกษตรกรรม|tr|Tarım toplumu|uk|Аграрне суспільство|ur|زرعی معاشرہ|vi|Xã hội nông nghiệp|zh|農業社會|qid=Q396108|lt=agrarian}} {{ill|Yayoi people|br|Poblad Yayoi|id|Orang Yayoi|it|Yayoi (popolo)|ja|弥生人|ko|야요이인|ms|Orang Yayoi|sl|Jajoji|sr|Јајои|th|ชาวยาโยอิ|tr|Yayoiler|ur|یایوئے لوگ|zh|彌生人|qid=Q19921451|lt=Yayoi}} tribes who came into conflict with indigenous {{ill|Jōmon people|br|Poblad Jōmon|ca|Jōmon|fa|مردمان جومون|id|Orang Jōmon|it|Jōmon (popolo)|ja|縄文人|ko|조몬인|my|ဂျိုမွန်လူမျိုး|pt|Jomons|sl|Ljudstvo Džomon|sr|Џомон (народ)|tr|Jōmonlar|zh|繩文人|qid=Q11608110|lt=Jōmon}} hunter-gatherers,<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Tanaka|first1=Atsuko|script-title=ja:古社叢の「聖地」の構造（3）─諏訪大社の場合|journal=Journal of Kyoto Seika University|pages=122–123|url=http://www.kyoto-seika.ac.jp/researchlab/wp/wp-content/uploads/kiyo/pdf-data/no39/tanaka_atsuko.pdf|language=ja|access-date=November 9, 2019|archive-date=July 22, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210722115610/https://www.kyoto-seika.ac.jp/researchlab/wp/wp-content/uploads/kiyo/pdf-data/no39/tanaka_atsuko.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="NHK">{{cite AV media|title=古代史ミステリー 「御柱」～最後の"縄文王国"の謎～ (Kodaishi Mystery. Onbashira: Saigo no Jōmon-ōkoku no nazo)|medium=Documentary|publisher=NHK|location=Japan|date=2016|url=http://www.nhk.or.jp/docudocu/program/46/2586790/|language=ja|access-date=November 9, 2019|archive-date=July 8, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190708025134/http://www.nhk.or.jp/docudocu/program/46/2586790/|url-status=dead}}</ref> others instead propose this conflict to have taken place during the late [[Kofun period]] (late 6th-early 7th century), when keyhole-shaped [[Kofun|Kofuns]] containing {{ill|Horse tack|ar|عدة الفرس|bat_smg|Kinkėmā|cs|Jezdecké potřeby|cv|Ут хатĕрĕ|fa|افسار|fr|Harnachement du cheval|hu|Lószerszám|id|Abah-abah|io|Harnesaro|is|Reiðtygi|it|Finimenti|ja|馬具|ko|마구|lt|Pakinktai|nl|Paardentuig|pl|Rząd koński|ro|Harnașament|ru|Сбруя|scn|Finalitati|sv|Hästutrustning|tr|At koşum takımı|tt|Дирбия|uk|Збруя|uz|Noʻxta|wa|Haernaxhmint|qid=Q950799|lt=equestrian gear}} as grave goods - up to this point found mainly in the {{ill|Shimoina District, Nagano|de|Shimoina-gun|fa|ناحیه شیموینا، ناگانو|fi|Shimo-Inan piirikunta|fr|District de Shimoina|it|Distretto di Shimoina|ja|下伊那郡|ko|시모이나군|pl|Powiat Shimoina|uk|Повіт Сімо-Іна|zh|下伊那郡|qid=Q726999|lt=Shimoina region}} southwest of Suwa - begin to appear in the Lake Suwa area, replacing the kind of burial that had been common in the region since the early 5th century. This theory thus supposes these migrants to have been a clan allied with the {{ill|Yamato period|ar|فترة ياماتو|be|Ямата (перыяд)|bg|Ямато (период)|ca|Període Yamato|ckb|سەردەمی یەماتۆ|cs|Období Jamato|de|Yamato-Zeit|eo|Epoko de Jamato|es|Período Yamato|fa|دوره یاماتو|fi|Yamato-kausi|fr|Période Yamato|he|תקופת יאמטו|hr|Yamato (razdoblje)|hu|Jamato-kor|id|Zaman Yamato|it|Periodo Yamato|ja|大和時代|ko|야마토 시대|ms|Zaman Yamato|nl|Yamatoperiode|pl|Yamato (okres)|ps|ياماتو|pt|Período Yamato|ro|Perioada Yamato|ru|Период Ямато|sh|Yamato period|sq|Periudha Jamato|sr|Јамато (период)|sv|Yamato (tidsperiod)|tl|Panahong Yamato|tr|Yamato Dönemi|uk|Період Ямато|vi|Thời kỳ Yamato|zh|大和時代|zh_min_nan|Yamato sî-tāi|qid=Q633881|lt=Yamato kingdom}} that specialized in horse breeding and horseback riding. Indeed, the Yamato polity showed strong interest to Shinano because of its suitability as a place for grazing and breeding horses and considered it a strategic base for conquering the eastern regions.<ref>Miyasaka (1987). pp. 18-22.</ref><ref>Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai, ed. (1995). p. 692.</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Terada |first1=Shizuko |last2=Washio |first2=Tetsuta |title=諏訪明神―カミ信仰の原像 (Suwa Myōjin: Kami shinkō no genzō)|date=2010 |publisher=Iwata Shoin |pages=64–67, 134–136}}</ref><ref>Oh (2011). pp. 156-157, 161-162, 176.</ref> This clan, the Miwa (Suwa), is thought to be related to either the Kanasashi clan (金刺氏), an offshoot of a local magnate clan (''[[kuni no miyatsuko]]'') that later became the high priestly family of the Lower Shrine of Suwa,<ref>Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai, ed. (1995). pp. 615-623, 686-696.</ref> or the Miwa (Ōmiwa) clan ([[:ja:三輪氏|三輪氏]]) originally based on the area around {{ill|Mount Miwa|arz|جبل مونت ميوا|ceb|Miwa Yama (bukid sa Hapon, Nara-ken)|de|Miwa (Berg)|es|Monte Miwa|fa|کوه میوا|fr|Mont Miwa|ja|三輪山|lld|Mont Miwa|my|မိဝတောင်|ru|Мива (гора)|zh|三輪山|qid=Q860627|lt=Mount Miwa}} in {{ill|Yamato Province|be|Ямата (правінцыя)|ca|Província de Yamato|ckb|پارێزگای یەماتۆ|cs|Provincie Jamato|de|Provinz Yamato|el|Επαρχία Γιαμάτο|es|Provincia de Yamato|fa|ولایت یاماتو|fi|Yamaton provinssi|fr|Province de Yamato|gl|Provincia de Yamato|hak|Yamato-koet|id|Provinsi Yamato|it|Yamato (provincia)|ja|大和国|ko|야마토국|lt|Jamato žemė|nl|Yamato (provincie)|no|Yamato (provins)|pt|Província de Yamato|ro|Provincia Yamato|ru|Ямато (провинция)|simple|Yamato Province|sk|Jamato (provincia)|sr|Провинција Јамато|th|แคว้นยามาโตะ|tr|Yamato (vilayet)|uk|Провінція Ямато|ur|یاماتو صوبہ|zh|大和國|zh_min_nan|Yamato-kok|zh_yue|大和國|qid=Q907495|lt=Yamato Province}}.<ref>Terada; Washio (2010). pp. 136-138.</ref> The theory suggests based on archaeological evidence that the Miwa (Suwa) came to the Suwa Basin from Shimoina, making their way northwards along the [[Tenryū River]].<ref>Terada; Washio (2010). pp. 66-67, 134-136.</ref> In conjunction with this hypothesis, it is pointed out that in the ''Nobushige Gejō'' (believed to be the earliest attestation of this myth), the Suwa deity is said to have descended from heaven bringing with him bells, a {{ill|Bronze mirror|ca|Espill de bronze|es|Espejo de bronce|fr|Miroir en bronze|ja|銅鏡|ko|동경 (거울)|my|ကြေးမုံ|no|Bronsespeil|simple|Bronze mirror|uk|Бронзове дзеркало|zh|铜镜|qid=Q1041984|lt=mirror}}, a {{ill|Saddle|an|Siella (aparello)|ar|سرج|arc|ܣܪܓܐ|ast|Siella de montar|az|Yəhər|ba|Эйәр|bg|Седло|br|Dibr|ca|Sella de muntar|chy|Hova'ó'xestôtse|cs|Jezdecké sedlo|cv|Йĕнер|cy|Cyfrwy|da|Sadel|de|Reitsattel|diq|Zên|eo|Selo|es|Silla de montar|et|Sadul|eu|Zela|fa|زین|fi|Satula|fr|Selle (équitation)|fy|Seal (hynsteriden)|gl|Sela|ha|Sirdi|he|אוכף|hi|ज़ीन|hr|Sedlo|ht|Sèl (sou cheval)|hu|Nyereg|hy|Թամբ|id|Pelana|io|Selo|is|Hnakkur|ja|鞍|ka|უნაგირი|kk|Ер|kn|ಜೀನು|ko|안장|ky|Ээр|la|Ephippium|lt|Balnas|lv|Segli|min|Palano|mn|Эмээл|ms|Pelana|myv|Камбраз|nl|Zadel (dier)|nn|Sal til dyr|no|Sal (dyr)|pl|Siodło|pms|Sela|pt|Sela|ro|Șa|ru|Седло|sah|Ыҥыыр|scn|Sedda (equitazzioni)|sco|Saidle|sh|Sedlo|simple|Saddle|sk|Jazdecké sedlo|sq|Shala e kalërimit|sr|Седло|sv|Ridsadel|ta|சேணம்|tr|Eyer|uk|Сідло|ur|زین|uz|Egar|vi|Yên|war|Lingkuranan ha hayop|wuu|鞍|zh|鞍|zh_yue|馬鞍|qid=Q192249|lt=Saddle}} and a {{ill|Bridle|an|Capezana|ar|لجام|arc|ܦܓܘܕܬܐ|be|Аброць|bg|Юзда|br|Kabestr|ca|Brida|chy|Hóxâhtsenáesëö'o|csb|Ùzda|cv|Йĕвен|de|Zaumzeug|eo|Brido|es|Brida (equitación)|et|Valjad|eu|Brida (zaldia)|fa|لگام (اسب)|fi|Suitset|fr|Bride (équitation)|ha|Linzami|he|רסן|hu|Kantár|id|Tali kekang|io|Brido|it|Testiera|ja|頭絡|ka|აღვირი|kk|Шідер|ky|Жүгөн|li|Hoofstèl|lt|Kamanos (pakinktai)|mk|Узда|mn|Богоч|no|Bissel|os|Идон|pdc|Zaahm|pl|Ogłowie|ro|Căpăstru|ru|Узда|sah|Үүн|sco|Bridle|simple|Bridle|sl|Uzda|sv|Betsel|uk|Вуздечка|uz|Yugan|zh|马辔|qid=Q148558|lt=Bridle}}.<ref>Grumbach (2005). p. 188.</ref><ref>Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai, ed. (1995). p. 683.</ref><ref>Miyasaka (1987). p. 33.</ref>

[[File:Mononobe no Moriya.jpg|thumb|150px|{{ill|Mononobe no Moriya|fa|مونونوبه نو موریا|fr|Mononobe no Moriya|ja|物部守屋|nl|Mononobe no Moriya|pt|Mononobe no Moriya|ru|Мононобэ-но Мория|sh|Mononobe no Moriya|th|โมโนโนเบะ โนะ โมริยะ|uk|Мононобе но Морія|zh|物部守屋|zh_classical|物部守屋|qid=Q2424736|lt=Mononobe no Moriya}}]]
This theory that the legend of the Suwa deity's victory over Moriya reflects historical fact has recently come into question. Due to similarities between certain variants of this myth and medieval legends surrounding {{ill|Prince Shōtoku|ar|شوتوكو تايشي|azb|شوتوکو تایشی|be|Сётоку Тайсі|ca|Shotoku Taishi|cs|Princ Šótoku|de|Shōtoku|es|Shōtoku|fa|شاهزاده شوتوکو تایشی|fi|Shōtoku (prinssi)|fr|Shōtoku (prince du Japon)|hr|Shōtoku|hu|Sótoku japán régensherceg|id|Pangeran Shōtoku|it|Umayado|ja|聖徳太子|jv|Pangéran Shōtoku|ka|შოტოკუ|ko|쇼토쿠 태자|la|Shotoku Taishi|nl|Shotoku Taishi|no|Shotoku|pl|Shōtoku (książę)|pt|Shōtoku Taishi|ro|Shōtoku|ru|Сётоку (принц)|sh|Princ Shōtoku|sq|Shotoku Taishi|sr|Принц Шотоку|sv|Prins Shōtoku|th|เจ้าชายโชโตกุ|tr|Prens Shōtoku|uk|Принц Сьотоку|vi|Thánh Đức Thái tử|zh|聖德太子|zh_classical|聖德太子|zh_min_nan|Sèng-tek Thài-chú|qid=Q263972|lt=Prince Shōtoku}}'s defeat of {{ill|Mononobe no Moriya|fa|مونونوبه نو موریا|fr|Mononobe no Moriya|ja|物部守屋|nl|Mononobe no Moriya|pt|Mononobe no Moriya|ru|Мононобэ-но Мория|sh|Mononobe no Moriya|th|โมโนโนเบะ โนะ โมริยะ|uk|Мононобе но Морія|zh|物部守屋|zh_classical|物部守屋|qid=Q2424736|lt=Mononobe no Moriya}} (e.g. Shōtoku's and Suwa Myōjin's opponents both being named 'Moriya', the deity's manifestation and the foundation of the Upper Shrine being dated to the year 587 - the same year as the {{ill|Soga–Mononobe conflict|fa|مناقشه سوگا–مونونوبه|fr|Bataille de Shigisan|id|Konflik Soga-Mononobe|ja|丁未の乱|ko|정미의 난|sh|Bitka kod Shigisana|vi|Chính biến Teibi|zh|丁未之亂|qid=Q534720|lt=battle}} between the [[Soga clan|Soga]] and the [[:en:Mononobe|Mononobe]] clans - in some texts), some see the myth as being highly influenced by such stories about Shōtoku (so Ihara, 2008),<ref>Ihara (2008). p. 161-162.</ref> while others regard it as an outright invention modeled on these legends (Harada, 2018).<ref>Harada (2018) p. 81.</ref> Aoki (2012) theorizes that the myth developed somewhere during the late Heian and early {{ill|Kamakura period|ar|فترة كاماكورا|be|Перыяд Камакура|bg|Камакура|bn|কামাকুরা যুগ|ckb|سەردەمی کاماکورا|cs|Období Kamakura|de|Kamakura-Zeit|eo|Kamakura-epoko|es|Período Kamakura|et|Kamakura ajastu|eu|Kamakura aroa|fa|دوره کاماکورا|fi|Kamakura-kausi|fr|Époque de Kamakura|gl|Período Kamakura|he|תקופת קמקורה|hu|Kamakura-kor|id|Zaman Kamakura|it|Periodo Kamakura|ja|鎌倉時代|ko|가마쿠라 시대|lt|Kamakura laikotarpis|mn|Камакура эрин|nl|Kamakuraperiode|no|Kamakura-perioden|pt|Período Kamakura|ru|Период Камакура|simple|Kamakura period|sk|Obdobie Kamakura|sl|Obdobje Kamakura|sr|Камакура период|sv|Kamakura|th|ยุคคามากูระ|tl|Panahong Kamakura|tr|Kamakura Dönemi|uk|Період Камакура|vi|Thời kỳ Kamakura|wuu|镰仓时代|zh|鎌倉時代|zh_min_nan|Kamakura sî-tāi|zh_yue|鎌倉時代|qid=Q236205|lt=Kamakura}} periods, when the deity of Suwa came to be venerated as a warrior god, and cautions against uncritical application of this story to known archaeological data.<ref>Aoki (2012). pp. 26-31.</ref>

===Takeminakata in imperial sources===
While the ''Kojiki'' does not yet explicitly mention the worship of Takeminakata in Suwa, by the following century, we see the name applied to the god worshipped in what is now the Grand Shrine of Suwa: aside from the ''Kuji Hongi''<nowiki />'s (807-936 CE) reference to Takeminakata being enshrined in 'Suwa Shrine in Suwa {{ill|Districts of Japan|ar|مقاطعات اليابان|ca|Districtes del Japó|da|Distrikter i Japan|de|Gun (Japan)|eo|Distriktoj de Japanio|es|Distritos de Japón|fa|شهرستان‌های ژاپن|fr|District (Japon)|id|Distrik (Jepang)|ilo|Dagiti distrito ti Hapon|it|Distretti del Giappone|lt|Japonijos apskritys|ms|Daerah di Jepun|nl|Districten van Japan|pt|Distritos do Japão|ro|Districtele Japoniei|ru|Уезды Японии|simple|Districts of Japan|su|Distrik di Jepang|th|อำเภอของประเทศญี่ปุ่น|tr|Japonya'nın ilçeleri|uk|Повіти Японії|ur|جاپان کے اضلاع|vi|Huyện của Nhật Bản|zh|郡 (日本)|qid=Q1122846|lt=District}}'<ref name="Hongi" /><ref name="Hongi2" /> the ''[[Shoku Nihon Kōki]]'' mentions the deity 'Minakatatomi-no-Kami of Suwa District, Shinano Province' (信濃国諏訪郡 ... 南方刀美神) being promoted from Rankless (无位) to junior fifth Rank, lower grade (従五位下) by the imperial court in the year 842 CE ({{ill|Jōwa (Heian period)|de|Jōwa|es|Jōwa (período Heian)|fa|جووا (دوره هی‌آن)|fr|Ère Jōwa (Heian)|ia|Jowa|id|Jōwa|ja|承和 (日本)|ko|조와 (834년)|ru|Дзёва Database)|publisher=Kokugakuin University}}</ref><ref name="Suwa689">Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai, ed. (1995). p. 689.</ref>

During the 850-60s, Takeminakata and his shrine rose very rapidly in Rank (''[[Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku|Montoku Jitsuroku]]'', ''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]''), being promoted to the Rank of junior fifth, upper grade (従五位上) in 850 ({{ill|Kashō|de|Kachō|es|Kashō|fa|کاشو (دوره)|fr|Ère Kashō|ia|Kajo|id|Kajō|ja|嘉祥|ko|가쇼 (848년)|ru|Кадзё (848—851)|simple|Kashō (early Heian period)|sr|Кашо (ера)|tr|Kashō|uk|Кадзьо (ненґо)|zh|嘉祥 (日本)|zh_yue|嘉祥 (年號)|qid=Q1373157|lt=Kashō}} 3),{{efn|「己未。信濃國御名方富命神、健御名方富命前八坂刀賣命神、並加從五位上。」}}<ref name="Montoku">{{cite wikisource |chapter=卷第二 |wslink=zh:日本文德天皇實錄 |plaintitle=''[[Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku]]'' (日本文德天皇實錄)}}</ref> to junior third (従三位) in 851 ({{ill|Ninju|de|Ninju|es|Ninju|fa|نینجو|fr|Ère Ninju|ia|Ninju|id|Ninju|ja|仁寿|ko|닌주|ru|Ниндзю|simple|Ninju|sr|Нинџу|tr|Ninju|uk|Ніндзю|zh|仁壽 (日本)|zh_yue|仁壽 (日本)|qid=Q1373077|lt=Ninju}} 1),{{efn|「乙丑。進信濃國建御名方富命、前八坂刀賣命等兩大神階、加從三位。」}}<ref name="Montoku2">{{cite wikisource |chapter=卷第三 |wslink=zh:日本文德天皇實錄 |plaintitle=''[[Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku]]'' (日本文德天皇實錄)}}</ref> to junior (従二位){{efn|「廿七日甲申。 (...) 信濃國正三位勳八等建御名方冨命神從二位。」}} and then senior second (正二位){{efn|「十一日丁酉。(...) 授信濃國從二位勳八等建御名方富命神正二位。」}} in 859 ({{ill|Jōgan|de|Jōgan|es|Jōgan|fa|جوگان|fr|Ère Jōgan|ia|Jogan|id|Jōgan|ja|貞観 (日本)|ko|조간 (연호)|ru|Дзёган|simple|Jōgan|sr|Џоган|tr|Jōgan|uk|Дзьоґан (ненґо)|zh|貞觀 (日本)|zh_yue|貞觀 (日本)|qid=Q1075635|lt=Jōgan}} 1),<ref name="NihonSandai">{{cite wikisource |chapter=卷第十 |wslink=zh:日本三代實錄 |plaintitle=''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]'' (日本三代實錄)}}</ref> and finally to junior first Rank (従一位) in 867 (Jōgan 9).{{efn|「十一日辛亥。信濃國正二位勳八等建御名方富命神進階從一位。」}}<ref name="NihonSandai2">{{cite wikisource |chapter=卷第十四 |wslink=zh:日本三代實錄 |plaintitle=''[[Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku]]'' (日本三代實錄)}}</ref><ref name="Database" /> The influence of the Kanasashi-no-toneri clan is thought to be behind the deity's sudden progress in Rank.<ref name="Suwa689" /><ref name="Owa221">Ōwa (1990). p. 221-223.</ref>

After a few decades, the 'Register of Deities' (神名帳 ''Jinmyōchō'') section of the ''[[Engishiki]]'' (927) speaks of the 'Minakatatomi Shrine(s)' (南方刀美神社) as enshrining two deities and being the two {{ill|Myōjin|fr|Myōjin|ja|明神|ko|묘진|zh|明神|qid=Q5369590|lt=major ('eminent') shrines}} of Suwa district.{{efn|「諏方郡<sub>二座 並大</sub> 南方刀美神社<sub>二座 名神大</sub>」}}<ref>{{cite web|title=Engishiki, vol. 10 (延喜式 第十巻)|url=https://jhti.berkeley.edu/cgi-bin/jhti/image.cgi?page=9&kan=10&honname=3|website=Japanese Historical Text Initiative (JHTI)|access-date=2019-08-23}}</ref> By 940 ({{ill|Tengyō|de|Tengyō|fa|تنگیو|fr|Ère Tengyō|ia|Tengyo|id|Tengyō|ja|天慶|ko|덴교|ru|Тэнгё|simple|Tengyō|sr|Тенгјо|tr|Tengyō|uk|Тенґьо (ненґо)|zh|天慶 (日本)|zh_yue|天慶 (日本)|qid=Q1327340|lt=Tengyō}} 3), the deity had been promoted to the highest Rank of senior first (正一位).<ref name="Suwa689" /><ref>{{cite web|title=社家の姓氏-諏訪氏-|url=http://www.harimaya.com/o_kamon1/syake/middle/s_suwa.html|website=播磨屋 (www.harimaya.com)}}</ref>

==Consort and Offspring==

[[File:Suwa taisha akimiya01bs3200.jpg|thumb|left|The ''Akimiya'' (秋宮) or Autumn Shrine, one of the two component shrines of the Suwa ''Shimosha'']]

===Yasakatome===

Suwa Myōjin's spouse is the goddess {{nihongo|'''[[Yasakatome|Yasakatome-no-Kami]]'''|八坂刀売神}}, most often considered to be the deity of the Lower Shrine of Suwa or the ''Shimosha''.<ref>Muraoka (1969). pp. 5–6.</ref> Unlike the relatively well-documented Suwa ''Kamisha'', very little concrete information is available regarding the origins of the ''Shimosha'' and its goddess.<ref>Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai, ed. (1995). p. 696.</ref>

[[Yasakatome]]'s first historical attestation is in the ''Shoku Nihon Kōki'', where the goddess is given the Rank of junior fifth, lower grade (従五位下) by the imperial court in the tenth month of {{ill|Jōwa (Heian period)|de|Jōwa|es|Jōwa (período Heian)|fa|جووا (دوره هی‌آن)|fr|Ère Jōwa (Heian)|ia|Jowa|id|Jōwa|ja|承和 (日本)|ko|조와 (834년)|ru|Дзёва (Хэйан)|simple|Jōwa (Heian period)|sr|Џова (Хејан период)|tr|Jōwa (Heian)|uk|Дзьова (ненґо)|zh|承和 (日本)|zh_yue|承和|qid=Q1075605|lt=Jōwa}} 9 (842 CE), five months after the same Rank was conferred on Takeminakata.{{efn|「奉授安房國從五位下安房大神正五位下。无位第一后神天比理刀咩命神。信濃國无位健御名方富命前八坂刀賣神。阿波國无位葦稻葉神。越後國无位伊夜比古神。常陸國无位筑波女大神竝從五位下。」}}<ref name="Shoku1" /><ref>{{cite web|title=南方刀美神社二座（八坂刀売命神）|url=http://21coe.kokugakuin.ac.jp/db/jinja/kindex2.php?J_ID=240201|website=神社資料データベース (Shinto Jinja Database)|publisher=Kokugakuin University}}</ref> As Takeminakata rose up in Rank, so did [[Yasakatome]],<ref>Miyasaka (1987). pp. 37-38.</ref><ref name="Montoku" /><ref name="Montoku2" /><ref name="NihonSandai" /> so that by 867 CE, [[Yasakatome]] had been promoted to senior second (正二位).<ref name="NihonSandai2" /> The goddess was finally promoted to senior first Rank (正一位) in 1074 ({{ill|Jōhō|fa|جوهو|fr|Ère Jōhō|ia|Joho|id|Jōhō|ja|承保|ko|조호 (1074년)|ru|Дзёхо|simple|Jōhō|sr|Џохо|tr|Jōhō|zh|承保|zh_yue|承保|qid=Q1193592|lt=Jōhō}} 1).<ref name="Owa221" />

Stories and claims about the goddess are diverse and contradictory. Regarding her parentage for instance, the lore of Kawaai Shrine (川会神社) in [[:en:Kitaazumi District|Kitaazumi District]] identifies [[Yasakatome]] as the daughter of {{ill|Watatsumi|abstract|Q1474187|az|Vatatsumi|de|Watatsumi|es|Watatsumi|fa|واتاتسومی|fr|Watatsumi|hu|Vatacumi|it|Watatsumi|ja|ワタツミ|ko|와타쓰미|mni|ꯋꯇꯠꯁꯨꯃꯤ|pl|Watatsumi|ru|Ватацуми|simple|Watatsumi|uk|Вататсумі|zh|綿津見|qid=Q1474187|lt=Watatsumi}}, god of the sea,<ref>{{cite web|title=八坂刀売神（ヤサカトメノカミ|url=http://japangod.dip.jp/%E5%85%AB%E5%9D%82%E5%88%80%E5%A3%B2%E7%A5%9E.html|website=日本の神様辞典 (Nihon no Kamisama Jiten)|access-date=May 27, 2017|archive-date=June 25, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170625160608/http://japangod.dip.jp/%E5%85%AB%E5%9D%82%E5%88%80%E5%A3%B2%E7%A5%9E.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>
which has been seen as hinting to a connection between the goddess and the seafaring [[Azumi people|Azumi clan]] ([[:ja:阿曇氏|安曇氏]]).<ref name="Miyasaka39">Miyasaka (1987). p. 39.</ref> Another claim originating from sources dating from the {{ill|Edo period|ar|فترة إيدو|ast|Periodu Edo|az|Edo dövrü|bcl|Panahon nin Edo|be|Перыяд Эда|bg|Едо (период)|bn|এদো যুগ|bo|ཨེ་དོའི་དུས་སྐབས།|br|Marevezh Edo|ca|Període Edo|ckb|سەردەمی ئێدۆ|cs|Období Edo|cv|Эдо тапхăрĕ|da|Edo-perioden|de|Edo-Zeit|el|Περίοδος Έντο|eo|Epoko de Edo|es|Período Edo|et|Edo ajastu|eu|Edo aroa|fa|دوره ادو|fi|Edo-kausi|fr|Époque d'Edo|gl|Período Edo|he|תקופת אדו|hi|एदो अवधी|hr|Edo (razdoblje)|hu|Edo-kor|id|Zaman Edo|is|Jedótímabilið|it|Periodo Edo|ja|江戸時代|jv|Jaman Édo|ko|에도 시대|lt|Edo laikotarpis|lv|Edo periods|mk|Едо (период)|mn|Эдогийн эрин|ms|Zaman Edo|new|इदो काल|nl|Edoperiode|nn|Edotida|oc|Periòde Edo|pl|Edo (okres)|pt|Período Edo|ro|Perioada Edo|ru|Период Эдо|simple|Edo period|sk|Obdobie Edo|sl|Obdobje Edo|sq|Periudha Edo|sr|Едо период|su|Période Edo|sv|Edoperioden|th|ยุคเอโดะ|tl|Panahong Edo|tok|tenpo pi kulupu lawa Eto|tr|Edo Dönemi|uk|Період Едо|ur|ایڈو دور|uz|Edo davri|vi|Thời kỳ Edo|war|Panahon Edo|wuu|江戶時代|zh|江户时代|zh_min_nan|Edo sî-tāi|zh_yue|江戶時代|qid=Q184963|lt=Edo period}} is that [[Yasakatome]] was the daughter of Ame-no-yasakahiko (天八坂彦命), a god recorded in the ''Kuji Hongi'' as one of the companions of [[List of Japanese deities#Minor kami|Nigihayahi-no-Mikoto]] when the latter came down from heaven.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Ponsonby-Fane|first1=R. A. B.|title=Studies in Shinto & Shrines|date=2014|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1136893018|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UVO4AwAAQBAJ&pg=PT148}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=先代舊事本紀卷第三 天神本紀|url=https://miko.org/~uraki/kuon/furu/text/sendaikuji/sendaikuji03.htm|website=私本 先代舊事本紀}}</ref><ref name="Miyasaka39" />

The ice cracks that appear on Lake Suwa during cold winters, the ''omiwatari'' ([[#Omiwatari|see above]]) are reputed in folklore to be caused by Suwa Myōjin's crossing the frozen lake to visit [[Yasakatome]].<ref name="railways1922" />

====Princess Kasuga====

The Kōga Saburō legend identifies the goddess of the Shimosha with Saburō's wife, whose name is given in some variants of the story as 'Princess Kasuga' (春日姫 ''Kasuga-hime'').<ref name="SuwaEngi">諏訪縁起の事 (''Suwa engi-no-koto'') in {{cite book|author=Kishi, Shōzō (trans.)|title=Shintōshū (神道集)|series=Tōyō Bunko (東洋文庫) vol. 94|date=1967|publisher=Heibonsha|isbn=978-4-582-80094-4|pages=238–286}}</ref><ref name="Kanai17">Kanai (1982). p. 17.</ref>

===Children===

In Suwa, a number of local deities are popularly considered to be the children of Suwa Myōjin and his consort. Ōta (1926) lists the following gods:<ref name="Ota4445">Ōta (1926). pp. 44–45.</ref>

[[File:Suwa taisha Kamisha Honmiya , 諏訪大社 上社 本宮 - panoramio (19).jpg|thumb|Izuhaya-sha (出早社), an [[Setsumatsusha|auxiliary shrine]] in the ''Kamisha Honmiya'' dedicated to the god Izuhayao (出早雄命), believed to be one of Suwa Myōjin's offspring]]
*Hikokamiwake-no-Mikoto (彦神別命)
*Tatsuwakahime-no-Kami (多都若姫神)
*Tamaru-hime-no-Kami (多留姫神) 
*Izuhayao-no-Mikoto (伊豆早雄命)
*Tateshina-no-Kami (建志名神)
*Tsumashinahime-no-Kami (妻科姫神)
*Ikeno'o-no-Kami (池生神)
*Tsumayamizuhime-no-mMikoto (都麻屋美豆姫命)
*Yakine-no-Mikoto (八杵命)
*Suwa-wakahiko-no-Mikoto (洲羽若彦命)
*Katakurabe-no-Mikoto (片倉辺命)
*Okihagi-no-Mikoto (興波岐命)
*Wakemizuhiko-no-Mikoto (別水彦命)
*Moritatsu-no-Kami (守達神)
*Takamori-no-kami (高杜神)
*Enatakemimi-no-Mikoto (恵奈武耳命)
*Okutsuiwatate-no-Kami (奥津石建神)
*Ohotsuno-no-Kami (竟富角神)
*Ōkunugi-no-Kami (大橡神)

===Claimed descendants===

====Suwa clan====

{{see also|Suwa clan}}

[[File:Jinchoukan-Moriya-shiryoukan_Oohouri-bosho.JPG|thumb|230px|right|The graves of various Suwa ''ōhōri'' within the historical estate grounds of the Moriya clan in Chino, Nagano. Both the [[:ja:神長官守矢史料館|Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum]] and the head [[Mishaguji]] shrine (''sōsha'') are located in the same precincts.]]
The [[Suwa clan]] who once occupied the position of head priest or ''ōhōri'' of the Suwa ''Kamisha'' traditionally considered themselves to be descendants of Suwa Myōjin/Takeminakata,<ref name="Picken">{{cite book|last1=Picken|first1=Stuart D.B.|title=Historical Dictionary of Shinto|date=December 28, 2010 |publisher=Scarecrow Press|isbn=978-0-8108-7172-4|page=288|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xlG3F6gSm9UC&pg=PA288}}</ref><ref name="Inoue352">Inoue (2003). p. 352.</ref><ref>{{cite book|author=Rekishi REAL Henshūbu (歴史REAL編集部) (ed.)|title=Jinja to kodai gōzoku no nazo (神社と古代豪族の謎)|date=2016|publisher=Yosensha|isbn=978-4800308924|page=40|language=ja}}</ref> although historically they are probably descended from the Kanasashi-no-toneri clan appointed by the Yamato court to govern the Suwa area in the 6th century ([[#Analysis|see above]]).<ref>Kanai (1982). pp. 14, 106-109.</ref>

====Other clans====

The Suwa ''ōhōri'' was assisted [[Suwa taisha#Kamisha|by five priests]], some of whom were also considered to be descendants of local deities related to Suwa Myōjin/Takeminakata.<ref name="Inoue352" /> One clan, the Koide (小出氏), the original occupants of the offices of ''negi-dayū'' (禰宜大夫) and ''gi-no-hōri'' (擬祝), claimed descent from the god Yakine.<ref>Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai, ed. (1995). p. 728, 731.</ref><ref name="Oota1924">{{cite book|author=Ōta, Akira|title=日本國誌資料叢書 信濃 (Nihon kokushi shiryō sōsho: Shinano)|date=1924|location=Tokyo|publisher=Isobe Kōyōdō|url=http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/982145/84|page=164}}</ref> A second clan, the Yajima (八島(嶋)氏 or 矢島氏), which served as ''gon-no-hōri'' (権祝), considered the god Ikeno'o to be their ancestor.<ref>Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai, ed. (1995). p. 730.</ref><ref name="Sasamoto">{{cite book|last1=Sasamoto|first1=Shōji|title=山をめぐる信州史の研究 (Yama wo meguru Shinshū-shi no kenkyū)|date=2003|publisher=Kōshi-shoin|isbn=978-4-906641-66-6|page=72}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=茅野市神長官守矢史料館 (Chino-shi Jinchōkan Moriya Shiryōkan)|url=http://www.suwa-tourism.jp/archives/000733.php|website=信州諏訪観光ナビ}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Ōta|date=1924|title=Nihon kokushi shiryō sōsho: Nagano|page=160}}</ref>

==Worship==
===Shrines===
As the gods of the Grand Shrine of Suwa, Suwa Myōjin/Takeminakata and [[Yasakatome]] also serve as the deities of shrines belonging to the Suwa shrine network (諏訪神社 ''Suwa-jinja'') all over Japan.

===As god of wind and water===

[[File:Nagikama.png|thumb|right|''Nagikama'']]The ''Nihon Shoki''<nowiki />'s record of Yamato emissaries worshipping the god of Suwa alongside the gods of [[Tatsuta Taisha|Tatsuta Shrine]] - worshipped for their power to control and ward off wind-related disasters such as {{ill|Drought|af|Droogte|ar|قحط|ast|Seca|ay|Awti Paru|uk|Тайфун|uz|Tayfun|vi|Bão nhiệt đới Tây Bắc Thái Bình Dương|wuu|风飔|za|Rumzhwx|zh|颱風|zh_min_nan|Hong-thai|zh_yue|颱風|qid=Q140588|lt=Typhoon}}s<ref>Hall, ed. (1988). p. 531.</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Tyler|first1=Royall|title=Japanese No Dramas|date=1992|publisher=Penguin UK|isbn=978-0141907802|page=cclvi|url=https://archive.org/details/japanesendramas0000tyle|url-access=registration}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Bock|first1=Felicia Gressitt|title=Engi-shiki; Procedures of the Engi Era: Books VI-X|date=1972|publisher=Sophia University|page=73}}</ref> - implies that the Yamato imperial court recognized the deity as a god of {{ill|List of wind deities|fr|Liste des divinités du vent|ja|風神一覧|tr|Rüzgâr tanrıları listesi|zh|風神列表|qid=Q51845481|lt=wind}} and {{ill|List of water deities|bn|জলদেবতার তালিকা|fa|اسامی ایزدان آب|szy|Kabit|th|รายพระนามเทพแห่งน้ำ|tr|Su tanrıları listesi|qid=Q13416336|lt=water}} during the late 7th century.<ref name="Yazaki22">{{cite book|editor1-last=Yazaki|editor1-first=Takenori|title=諏訪大社 (Suwa-taisha)|date=1986|publisher=Ginga shobō|series=Ginga gurafikku sensho|volume=4|page=22|language=ja}}</ref><ref name="Muraoka17">Muraoka (1969). p. 17.</ref> One theory regarding the origin of the name '(Take)minakata' even supposes it to derive from a word denoting a body of water (水潟 ''minakata''; [[#Etymology|see above]]).<ref name="Miyasaka31" /><ref name="Okada" /><ref>Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai, ed. (1995). p. 686.</ref>

Snake-shaped iron [[:en:Kama (weapon)|sickle]] blades called ''nagikama'' (薙鎌) were traditionally used in the Suwa region to ward off strong winds, typhoons and other natural disasters; it was once customary for ''nagikama'' to be attached to wooden staves and placed on one corner of the rooftop of the house during the autumn typhoon season.<ref name="Yazaki98" /><ref>Miyasaka (1992). pp. 172-173.</ref><ref>Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai, ed. (1995). p. 677.</ref> ''Nagikama'' are also traditionally hammered onto the trees chosen to become the ''{{ill|Onbashira|es|Onbashira|fr|Onbashira|ja|御柱祭|ru|Омбасира|vi|Onbashira|qid=Q3698846|lt=Onbashira}}'' of the Suwa ''Kamisha'' and ''Shimosha'' some time before these are actually felled.<ref>Miyasaka (1992). pp. 164-172.</ref> In addition to these and other uses, the blades are also distributed to function as ''[[shintai]]'' for branch shrines of the [[Shinto shrine#Shrine networks|Suwa shrine network]].<ref name="Yazaki98">Yazaki, ed. (1986). pp. 98-100.</ref><ref>Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai, ed. (1995). p. 674.</ref>

===Association with snakes and dragons===

Suwa Myōjin's association with the {{ill|Snakes in mythology|ar|الثعابين في الأساطير|ce|Лаьхьа (мифологи)|fr|Serpents dans la mythologie|nl|Slangen in de cultuur|ru|Змей|uk|Змій (міфологія)|qid=Q16326794|lt=snake}} or the {{ill|Japanese dragon|ar|تنين ياباني|as|জাপানী ড্ৰেগন|ca|Drac japonès|es|Dragón japonés|fa|اژدهای ژاپنی|gl|Dragón xaponés|hu|Japán sárkány|ia|Dracon japonese|it|Drago giapponese|ja|日本の竜|ko|일본의 용|mk|Јапонски змејови|ms|Naga Jepun|nl|Japanse draak|pl|Smok japoński|pt|Dragão japonês|ro|Dragon japonez|ru|Японский дракон|simple|Japanese dragon|tl|Dragong Hapones|tr|Japon ejderhası|uk|Японський дракон|vi|Rồng Nhật Bản|zh|日本的龍|qid=Q2366503|lt=dragon}} in many stories featuring the god such as the Kōga Saburō legend (see [[#Legends of Suwa Myōjin|'Legends of Suwa Myōjin']] above) might be related to his being considered as a deity presiding over wind and water, due to the association of dragons with winds and the rain in Japanese belief.<ref>Kanai (1982). pp. 4-7.</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=De Visser|first1=Marinus Willem|title=The Dragon in China and Japan|date=1913|page=153|publisher=Cosimo |isbn=9781605204093 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Mpg6Xd2jW2YC&pg=PA153}}</ref> (See also ''[[mizuchi]]''.)

[[File:Samantabhadra_Fugen_Bosatsu_Okura.JPG|thumb|left|170px|Suwa Myōjin was once believed to be a manifestation (''suijaku'') of the bodhisattva Samantabhadra.]]

(who is sometimes identified with Samantabhadra) - and a sanctuary to Samantabhadra (普賢堂 ''Fugendō''), both of which served at the time as the ''Kamisha''<nowiki />'s [[Shintai|main objects of [[File:Suwa Kamisha Tettō.png|thumb|200px|The ''Kamisha Honmiya''<nowiki />'s Iron Tower or ''Tettō'' photographed during the early 20th century. After the removal or demolition of Buddhist structures in Suwa Shrine following the [[Shinbutsu bunri|separation of Buddhism and Shinto]], this pagoda was moved to Onsenji Temple (温泉寺) in {{ill|Suwa, Nagano|ar|سوا (ناغانو)|azb|سووا، ناقانو|ce|Сува (гӀала)|ceb|Suwa (lungsod)|de|Suwa (Nagano)|es|Suwa (Nagano)|fa|سووا، ناگانو|fi|Suwa|fr|Suwa (Nagano)|gl|Suwa|hy|Սուվա (քաղաք)|id|Suwa, Nagano|it|Suwa|ja|諏訪市|ko|스와시|mzn|سووا، ناگانو|nl|Suwa|pl|Suwa (miasto)|pt|Suwa (Nagano)|ro|Suwa|ru|Сува (город)|sv|Suwa, Nagano|tg|Сува|th|ซูวะ|tl|Suwa, Nagano|tr|Suwa|tt|Сува (шәһәр)|uk|Сува (Наґано)|ur|سووا، ناگانو|uz|Suva (Nagano)|vi|Suwa, Nagano|war|Suwa, Nagano|zh|諏訪市|zh_classical|諏訪市|zh_min_nan|Suwa-chhī|zh_yue|諏訪|qid=Q846338|lt=Suwa City}}, where it currently resides.]]

With the establishment of {{ill|State Shinto|bn|রাষ্ট্রীয় শিন্তৌ|de|Staats-Shintō|es|Sintoísmo estatal|fa|شینتوی حکومتی|fr|Shintoïsme d'État|id|Shinto Negara|ja|国家神道|ko|국가신토|no|Statsshinto|pt|Xintoísmo estatal|ru|Государственный синтоизм|simple|State Shinto|tr|Devlet Şintoizmi|vi|Thần đạo Quốc gia|zh|国家神道|qid=Q1197248|lt=State Shinto}} after the [[Meiji Restoration]] in 1868 and the subsequent [[Shinbutsu bunri|separation of Buddhism and Shinto]], the shrine monks (''shasō'') attached to Buddhist temples in the Suwa shrine complex were laicized, with Buddhist symbols and structures being either removed or destroyed; Buddhist ceremonies performed in both the ''Kamisha'' and the ''Shimosha'', such as the yearly offering of the {{ill|Lotus Sutra|af|Lotussoetra|bg|Лотосова сутра|bn|সদ্ধর্ম পুণ্ডরীক সূত্র|ca|Sutra del Lotus|cs|Lotosová sútra|de|Lotos-Sutra|eo|Sutro de la blanka lotuso de la sublima darmo|es|Sutra del loto|et|Lootossuutra|fa|سوره نیلوفر|fr|Sūtra du Lotus|hi|सद्धर्मपुण्डरीक सूत्र|hu|Lótusz szútra|id|Sutra Seroja|it|Sutra del Loto|ja|法華経|ko|묘법연화경|lt|Lotoso sūtra|ms|Sutra Teratai|nl|Lotussoetra|no|Lotussūtraen|pa|ਸਧਰਮਪੁੰਡਰੀਕ ਸੂਤਰ|pl|Sutra lotosu|pt|Sutra do Lótus|ru|Лотосовая сутра|sr|Лотосова сутра|sv|Lotussutran|ta|தாமரை சூத்திரம்|th|สัทธรรมปุณฑรีกสูตร|tr|Lotus Sutra|uk|Сутра Лотоса|ur|سددھرمہ پونڈریکہ سوترم|vi|Pháp hoa kinh|wuu|妙法莲华经|zh|妙法莲华经|zh_yue|妙法蓮華經|qid=Q861212|lt=en:Lotus Sutra}} to Suwa Myōjin (involving the placing of a copy of the sutra inside the ''Tettō''), were discontinued.<ref>Inoue (2003). pp. 362-371.</ref>

===As god of hunting===

Suwa Myōjin is also worshipped as a {{ill|List of hunting deities|ar|قائمة آلهة الصيد|pt|Lista de divindades da caça|tr|Av ilâhları listesi|qid=Q6623822|lt=god of hunting}}; not surprisingly, some of the ''Kamisha''<nowiki />'s religious ceremonies traditionally involve(d) ritual For instance, the Frog Hunting Ritual (蛙狩神事 ''kawazugari shinji'') held every New Year's Day involves the shooting (or rather, piercing) of frogs captured from a sacred river or stream within the ''Kamisha''<nowiki />'s precincts with miniature arrows.<ref name="Miyasaka9216">Miyasaka (1992). pp. 16-20.</ref><ref>Yazaki, ed. (1986). p. 72.</ref><ref>Tanigawa (1987). pp. 154-155.</ref> This ritual - which has come under harsh criticism from local activists and animal rights groups for its perceived cruelty to the frogs involved<ref>{{cite web|title=Suwa taisha skewering live frogs (生きたカエルを串刺しにする諏訪大社)|url=http://blog.livedoor.jp/liablog/archives/1790677.html|website=NGO Life Investigation Agency (LIA)|date=December 30, 2013 |access-date=2016-01-05}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Rabid animal rights activists go head-to-head with tradition|url=https://japantoday.com/Category/features/kuchikomi/rabid-animal-rights-activists-go-head-to-head-with-tradition|website=Japan Today|date=September 30, 2015 }}</ref> - was traditionally performed to secure peace and a bountiful harvest for the coming year.<ref name="Miyasaka9216" />

One of the Suwa ''Kamisha''<nowiki />'s hunting festivals, the Misayama Festival (御射山祭), formerly held in a field - the ''kōya'' (神野 'the god's plain') - at the foot of the [[Yatsugatake Mountains]] for five days (from the 26th to the 30th of [[Japanese calendar#Months|the seventh month]]),{{efn|Currently three days: from the 26th to the 28th of August.<ref>Tanigawa (1987). p. 157.</ref>}} was {{ill|Samurai|af|Samoerai|ar|ساموراي|as|ছামুৰাই|ast|Samurái|az|Samuray|ba|Самурай|bar|Samurai|bcl|Samurai|be|Самурай|be_x_old|Самурай|bg|Самурай|bn|সামুরাই|bo|ས་མུ་རའི།|br|Samourai|bs|Samuraj|bxr|Самурай|ca|Samurai|ceb|Samurai|ckb|سامورای|cs|Samuraj|cy|Samwrai|da|Samurai|de|Samurai|el|Σαμουράι|eo|Samurajo|es|Samurái|et|Samurai|eu|Samurai|fa|سامورایی|fi|Samurai|fr|Samouraï|frr|Samurai|fy|Samoerai|ga|Samúraí|gd|Samurai|gl|Samurai|glk|سامۊرايي|gn|Samurái|gu|સમુરાઇ|he|סמוראי|hi|सामुराई|hr|Samuraji|hu|Szamuráj|hy|Սամուրայ|ia|Samurai|id|Samurai|ie|Samurai|io|Samurayo|is|Samúræi|it|Samurai|ja|侍|jv|Samurai|ka|სამურაი|kk|Самурай|kn|ಸಮುರಾಯ್|ko|사무라이|ky|Самурай|la|Samuraeus|lmo|Samurai|ln|Samurai|lt|Samurajus|lv|Samuraji|mk|Самурај|ml|സാമുറായ്|mn|Самүрай|mnw|သာမူရာၚ်|mr|सामुराई|ms|Samurai|my|ဆာမူရိုင်း|mzn|سامورایی|nl|Samoerai|nn|Samurai|no|Samurai|oc|Samorai|pa|ਸੈਮੂਰਾਈ|pl|Samuraj|pnb|سیمورائی|ps|ساموراي|pt|Samurai|ro|Samurai|ru|Самурай|sah|Самурай|sc|Samurai|sh|Samuraj|simple|Samurai|sk|Samuraj|sl|Samuraj|sq|Samurai|sr|Самурај|su|Samurai|sv|Samuraj|ta|சாமுராய்|th|ซามูไร|tl|Samurai|tr|Samuray|uk|Самурай|ur|سامورائی|uz|Samuraylar|vi|Samurai|wa|Samouraye|war|Samurai|wuu|侍|xmf|სამურაი|yi|סאמוריי|zh|侍|zh_min_nan|Samurai|zh_yue|侍|qid=Q38142|lt=samurai class}} from all across Japan who engaged in displays of [[Yabusame|mounted archery]], bouts of [[:en:Sumo wrestling|Sumo wrestling]] and {{ill|Takagari|az|Takaqari|it|Takagari|qid=Q16933847|lt=falconry}} as part of the festivities, as well as people from all walks of life.<ref>Tanigawa (1987). pp. 159-160.</ref><ref>Yazaki, ed. (1986). pp. 76-77.</ref><ref>Miyasaka (1992). pp. 115-118.</ref> The ''Shimosha'' also held its own Misayama Festival at the same time as the ''Kamisha'' (albeit in a different location), in which various warrior clans also participated.<ref>Tanigawa (1987). pp. 158-159.</ref><ref>Miyasaka (1992). pp. 119-124.</ref>

Suwa Myōjin's association with the mountains and hunting is also evident from the description of the ''ōhōri'' as sitting upon a deer hide (the deer being an animal thought to be sacred to Suwa Myōjin) during the ''Ontōsai'' ritual as practiced during medieval times.<ref>Tanigawa (1987). p. 138.</ref><ref>Oh (2011). pp. 173.</ref>

====Suwa Myōjin and meat eating====

At a time when slaughter of animals and consumption of meat was frowned upon due to {{ill|Mahayana|af|Mahayana|ar|مهايانا|arz|ماهايانا|as|মহাযান|az|Mahayana|ban|Mahāyāna|bar|Mahayana|bcl|Mahayana|be|Махаяна|bg|Махаяна|bh|महायान|bn|মহাযান|bo|ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོ།|br|Mahayana|ca|Mahayana|ckb|ماھایانا|cs|Mahájána|cy|Mahayana|da|Mahayana|de|Mahayana|el|Μαχαγιάνα|eo|Mahajano|es|Mahāyāna|et|Mahajaana|eu|Mahāyāna|fa|مهایانه|fi|Mahajana|fr|Bouddhisme mahāyāna|fy|Mahayana|gcr|Boudism mahāyāna|gl|Mahayana|ha|Mahayana|he|מהאיאנה|hi|महायान|hr|Mahajana|hu|Mahájána|ia|Mahayana|id|Mahāyāna|ilo|Mahayana|is|Mahāyāna|it|Buddismo Mahāyāna|ja|大乗仏教|jam|Mahayaana|jv|Mahayana|ka|მაჰაიანა|kk|Махаяна|km|មហាយាន|ko|대승불교|ky|Махаяна|la|Mahayana|lld|Mahāyāna|lo|ມະຫາຍານ|lt|Mahajana|lv|Mahājāna|mag|महायान|mg|Bodisma mahaiana|mk|Махајана|ml|മഹായാനം|mn|Махаяна|mr|महायान|ms|Mahayana|mwl|Mahayana|my|မဟာယာန|mzn|مِئایانه|ne|महायान|new|महायान|nl|Mahayana|nn|Mahayana|no|Mahāyāna|oc|Bodisme mahayana|pa|ਮਹਾਯਾਨ|pl|Mahajana|pnb|مہایان|ps|مهايانا|pt|Maaiana|ro|Mahāyāna|ru|Махаяна|sa|महायानम्|sco|Mahayana|sh|Mahajana|si|මහායාන බුදු දහම|simple|Mahayana|sk|Mahájána|sq|Mahajana|sr|Махајана|sv|Mahayana|ta|மகாயான பௌத்தம்|te|మహాయానం|th|มหายาน|tl|Budismong Mahayana|tr|Mahayana|uk|Махаяна|ur|مہایان|uz|Mahayana|vi|Đại thừa|war|Mahayana|wuu|大乘佛教|zh|大乘佛教|zh_min_nan|Tāi-sēng Hu̍t-kàu|zh_yue|大乘佛教|qid=Q48362|lt=Mahayana}}'s [[Buddhist vegetarianism#Mahayana view|strict views on vegetarianism]] and [[Buddhist ethics#Killing|the general Buddhist opposition against the taking of life]], the cult of Suwa Myōjin was a unique feature in the Japanese religious landscape for its celebration of hunting and meat eating.<ref>Kanai (1982). p. 21-23.</ref>

A four-line verse attached to the Kōga Saburō legend popularly known as the ''Suwa no kanmon'' (諏訪の勘文) encapsulates the justification of meat eating within a Buddhist framework: by being eaten by humans and 'dwelling' inside their bodies, ignorant animals could achieve {{ill|Enlightenment in Buddhism|af|Verligting in Boeddhisme|ar|التنوير في البوذية|bcl|Kaliwanagan sa Budismo|bn|বোধোদয়|et|Virgumine|fa|روشنیدگی (بودیسم)|fr|Éveil (bouddhisme)|hu|Megvilágosodás a buddhizmusban|hy|Բուդդայական լուսավորություն|id|Pencerahan dalam Buddhisme|it|Illuminazione nel buddismo|ja|悟り|lt|Atbudimas (budizmas)|nl|Verlichting (boeddhisme)|no|Opplysning i buddhismen|ps|روښانتیا په بودیزم کې|ru|Просветление (буддизм)|simple|Enlightenment (Buddhism)|th|ตรัสรู้|uz|Buddizmda ma’rifat|vi|Giác ngộ trong Phật giáo|zh|开悟|qid=Q1137019|lt=enlightenment}} together with their human consumers.<ref>Kanai (1982). p. 22.</ref><ref>Miyasaka (1987). pp. 56-57.</ref>

{{Blockquote|text=<poem>業尽有情 ''Gōjin ujō''
雖放不生 ''Suihō fushō''
故宿人天 ''Koshuku ninten''
同証仏果 ''Dōshō bukka''<ref name="SuwaEngi" /><ref>See Kanai (1982). pp. 318-319 for attested variants.</ref>

Sentient beings who have exhausted their {{ill|Karma in Buddhism|ar|الكارما في البوذية|be_x_old|Карма ў будызьме|bg|Карма в будизма|bn|কর্ম (বৌদ্ধ দর্শন)|br|Karma (boudaegezh)|bs|Karma u budizmu|cs|Karma v buddhismu|fa|کارما در آیین بودا|hu|Karma a buddhizmusban|id|Karma dalam Buddhisme|km|ច្បាប់នៃកម្ម|mr|कर्म (बौद्ध धर्म)|my|ကံ|ne|कर्म (बौद्ध)|no|Karma i buddhismen|pl|Karma w buddyzmie|pt|Carma (budismo)|sh|Karma u budizmu|shn|ၵၢမ်ႇ|si|කර්ම (බුදු දහම අනුව)|sr|Карма (будизам)|th|กรรม (ศาสนาพุทธ)|vi|Nghiệp (Phật giáo)|zh|業 (佛教)|qid=Q2673416|lt=karma}}:
Even if one [[Animals in Buddhism#Release of animals|sets (them) free]], (they) will not live (for long);
Therefore (have them) dwell within humans and {{ill|Deva (Buddhism)|bn|দেব (বৌদ্ধধর্ম)|cs|Bohové (buddhismus)|es|Deva (budismo)|et|Deeva|fa|دوا (بودیسم)|hu|Déva (buddhizmus)|id|Dewa (Buddhisme)|ja|天部|km|ទេវតា(ពុទ្ធសាសនា)|ko|천 (불교)|lt|Devai (budizmas)|my|နတ်|nl|Boeddhistische goden|no|Deva (buddhisme)|pl|Dewa (buddyzm)|pt|Deva (budismo)|ro|Deva (Budism)|ru|Дэва (буддизм)|sl|Deve|ta|தேவர் (பௌத்தம்)|th|เทวดา (ศาสนาพุทธ)|uz|Deva (buddizm)|vi|Thiên (Phật giáo)|zh|天人 (佛教)|qid=Q4089509|lt=gods}}
(That they may) as well achieve {{ill|Buddhahood|ar|بوذوية|az|Buddalıq|bcl|Pagka-Buddha|blk|ဗုဒ္ဓ|bn|বুদ্ধ (উপাধি)|fa|بوداساتوا|fr|Buddhatva|hi|बुद्धत्व|hu|Buddhaság|ia|Buddhitate|id|Kebuddhaan|ja|成仏|kbd|Будда|ko|부처|lmo|Buddhitaa|mag|बुद्धत्व|mr|बुद्धत्व|my|ဗုဒ္ဓ|pi|बुद्धत्ता|rki|ဗုဒ္ဓ|si|බුදුවරු|sv|Buddhaskap|ur|بدھتو|vi|Phật thành|zh|成佛|qid=Q56247062|lt=Buddhahood}}</poem>}}

===As war god===
[[File:Hatajirushi3.png|180px|thumb|right|A depiction of war banners used by the [[Taira clan]] (right) and Takeda Shingen (left). The leftmost banner (white with blue border and red lettering) carries the inscription ''Suwa hosshō-kamishimo-daimyōjin'' (諏訪法性上下大明神).]]
[[File:Shingen_Takeda%27s_armour.jpg|180px|thumb|right|A modern reproduction of Takeda Shingen's helmet]]
Suwa Myōjin is also considered to be a {{ill|List of war deities|ar|قائمة آلهة الحرب|arz|الهة الحرب|et|Sõjajumal|pt|Deidade bélica|tr|Savaş tanrıları listesi|qid=Q1752560|lt=god of war}}, one of a number of such deities in the Japanese pantheon. Besides the legend of the god's apparition to [[Sakanoue no Tamuramaro]] ([[#Apparition to Sakanoue no Tamuramaro|see above]]), the ''[[:en:Songs to Make the Dust Dance on the Beams|Ryōjin Hishō]]'' compiled in 1179 (the late {{ill|Heian period|ar|فترة هييآن|ast|Periodu Heian|az|Heyan dövrü|bcl|Panahon ni Heian|bg|Хеян|bn|হেইআন যুগ|br|Marevezh Heian|ca|Període Heian|ceb|Panahon sa Heian|cs|Období Heian|de|Heian-Zeit|el|Περίοδος Χεϊάν|eo|Epoko Heian|es|Período Heian|eu|Heian aroa|fa|دوره هی‌آن|fi|Heian-kausi|fr|Époque de Heian|gl|Período Heian|he|תקופת הייאן|hi|हेआन काल|hr|Heian (razdoblje)|hu|Heian-kor|hy|Հեիան ժամանակաշրջան|id|Zaman Heian|it|Periodo Heian|ja|平安時代|ka|ჰეიანის პერიოდი|ko|헤이안 시대|la|Aevum Heian|lt|Hejano laikotarpis|mn|Хэйан|mr|हियन कालावधी|ms|Zaman Heian|my|ဟဲအိအန်ခေတ်|nl|Heianperiode|nn|Heian|no|Heian-perioden|oc|Epòca d'Heian|pl|Heian|ps|هېيان دوره|pt|Período Heian|ro|Perioada Heian|ru|Период Хэйан|sh|Heianski period|simple|Heian period|sk|Obdobie Heian|sl|Obdobje Heian|sq|Periudha Heian|sr|Хеиан период|sv|Heian|ta|ஹையன் காலகட்டம்|th|ยุคเฮอัง|tl|Panahong Heian|tr|Heian Dönemi|uk|Період Хейан|vi|Thời kỳ Heian|war|Panahon Heian|wuu|平安时代|zh|平安时代|zh_classical|平安朝|zh_min_nan|Heian sî-tāi|zh_yue|平安時代|qid=Q193292|lt=Heian period}}) also attest to the worship of the god of Suwa in the capacity of god of warfare at the time of its compilation, naming the shrine of Suwa among famous shrines to martial deities in the eastern half of the country.
